domains.name: Active Directory Security
domains.tagline: Map, audit, and score Active Directory attack paths — graph enumeration, Kerberos/protocol tooling, credential-exposure testing, and risk health checks — for authorized assessments and blue-team defense.

tools.name: BloodHound CE
tools.desc: The current-generation attack-path engine: ingests SharpHound data into a Neo4j graph and reveals how users, groups, computers, sessions, GPOs, ACLs, trusts, and ADCS enrollments chain into paths to Domain Admin — including ADCS, NTLM, and delegation abuse conditions.
tools.when: The core analysis step after collection: visualize and triage which abusable identity relationships are the shortest paths to Tier-0, and why they matter to defenders.
tools.install: wget https://github.com/SpecterOps/bloodhound-cli/releases/latest/download/bloodhound-cli-linux-amd64.tar.gz (see the CE Quickstart for the Docker-Compose deployment)

tools.name: SharpHound
tools.desc: C# data collector for BloodHound CE that runs on domain-joined Windows and exports a zip of users, groups, sessions, local admins, ACLs, GPOs, trusts, and more via LDAP and SMB — the dataset the graph is built from.
tools.when: Run first from any authorized domain-joined host or as a standalone binary, then feed the output into BloodHound CE for graph analysis.
tools.install: Download the SharpHound CE binary from the BloodHound CE UI (Settings → Download Collectors) or the GitHub releases page

tools.name: PlumHound
tools.desc: Wraps BloodHound's Neo4j Cypher backend into repeatable HTML reports and task lists; surfaces the busiest paths to Domain Admin and which relationship to break to sever a given path.
tools.when: Turn a collected BloodHound graph into consumable, operations-ready findings for blue/purple-team remediation planning and scheduled reporting.

tools.name: Impacket
tools.desc: Fortra's Python library of Windows network protocol implementations plus ~100 example scripts — secretsdump (remote SAM/LSA/NTDS credential extraction over DRSUAPI/DCOM/registry in mimikatz-compatible hash format), psexec/wmiexec/atexec remote execution, ntlmrelayx, and a full Kerberos toolbox.
tools.when: The foundation for nearly all Linux-side AD work: secretsdump is the standard way to audit credential hygiene on controllers and hosts during an authorized assessment.

tools.name: NetExec
tools.desc: The maintained successor to CrackMapExec: multi-protocol (SMB, LDAP, MSSQL, SSH, WinRM, RDP) credential validation that rapidly tests which identities work where, sprays passwords, and enumerates shares, users, sessions, domains, and password policy across a fleet.
tools.when: Fast credential-driven health-check across many hosts in one pass — who is effective as admin, which policy is weakest, and which shares are open.

tools.name: Kerbrute
tools.desc: Go tool that validates AD usernames and tests passwords through Kerberos AS-REQ/AS-REP exchanges; its userenum mode never triggers account lockout, while passwordspray/bruteforce do and are meant for policy-aware testing.
tools.when: Discover which candidate usernames actually exist during recon, and safely prove a single reused weak password across a user list you monitor in your own logs.

tools.name: Rubeus
tools.desc: C# toolset for raw Kerberos interaction — ticket requests and passthe-ticket, overpass-the-hash, golden/silver/diamond ticket forging, Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, and s4u delegation testing, compiled to run on Windows.
tools.when: Windows-side Kerberos validation: check which service accounts are Kerberoastable and how delegation and ticket caching expose lateral movement in your domain.
tools.install: Prebuilt binaries ship under Rubeus/Release — or compile with dotnet build against the repo source

tools.name: Mimikatz
tools.desc: The canonical Windows credential tool: sekurlsa extracts plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, PINs, and Kerberos tickets from LSASS memory, while lsadump covers SAM, LSA secrets, DCSync, and DCShadow, plus pass-the-hash/ticket and token manipulation.
tools.when: On an authorized host with local admin to prove whether LSASS-accessible credentials leak and whether protections like LSA Protection or Credential Guard actually hold.

tools.name: pypykatz
tools.desc: Pure-Python reimplementation of Mimikatz's sekurlsa: parses live LSASS memory or minidump files on any OS to recover NT hashes, plaintext credentials, Kerberos tickets, and DPAPI keys.
tools.when: Analyze an LSASS dump from Linux during incident response or assessment when you hold the dump rather than a live Windows host.

tools.name: lsassy
tools.desc: Python tool that remotely dumps LSASS (comsvcs, Procdump, nanodump, and more methods) over SMB/WMI from whole fleets at once and extracts credentials in place with pypykatz.
tools.when: When you hold admin on a set of Windows hosts and want to audit logged-on credential exposure across the fleet without interactive sessions on each box.

tools.name: PowerView
tools.desc: Pure-PowerShell AD enumerator (PowerSploit) turning LDAP into one-liner cmdlets for users, groups, computers, GPOs, ACLs, shares, and trust maps; also hunts which machines specific users log into and where you have local admin.
tools.when: From a domain-joined PowerShell session when you need fast, scriptable situational awareness without dropping a binary on disk — and to see exactly what attackers enumerate first.

tools.name: PowerUp
tools.desc: PowerSploit module that audits a Windows host for common local privilege-escalation misconfigurations — unquoted service paths, writable service binaries, modifiable services, AlwaysInstallElevated — and reports each with abuse-ready detail.
tools.when: Local privilege-escalation audit of a single host during sanctioned testing or as part of hardening a fleet that lacks LAPS and least-privilege discipline.

tools.name: BloodHound.py
tools.desc: Python/Impacket ingestor for BloodHound CE that collects users, computers, groups, trusts, ACLs, sessions, and local admins from Linux using only credentials — no Windows host or SharpHound binary required.
tools.when: When you need BloodHound data but have no Windows foothold; the Linux-native collection counterpart to SharpHound.
tools.install: pipx install bloodhound-ce (bloodhound-ce branch adds the bloodhound-ce-python CLI)

tools.name: PingCastle
tools.desc: Active Directory risk and maturity audit (by Netwrix) that scores a domain 0–100 across ~10 axes — accounts, ADCS, Kerberos, trusts, delegation, GPOs, infrastructure — and emits a CISO-ready HTML report with prioritized remediation via a read-only healthcheck.
tools.when: The default first formal AD security assessment: minutes to run, zero writes, and ideal as a recurring blue-team health check or engagement kickoff.
tools.install: Download standalone PingCastle.exe from https://github.com/netwrix/pingcastle/releases and run on a domain-joined Windows host (.NET 8)

tools.name: Purple Knight
tools.desc: Free commercial assessment from Semperis scoring hybrid AD, Entra ID, and Okta estates against 150+ indicators of exposure and compromise, with MITRE ATT&CK mapping and prioritized executive guidance.
tools.when: Complement PingCastle when you also manage Entra ID or Okta and want an easy scorecard plus IoC checks across the hybrid estate.
tools.install: Download the Windows agent from https://www.semperis.com/purple-knight/ (free registration required)

tools.name: ADRecon
tools.desc: PowerShell tool that extracts a wide slice of AD state — users, groups, OUs, GPOs, trusts, ACLs, password policies, DNS zones, and optionally LAPS/BitLocker keys and Kerberoastable SPNs — and consolidates it into a summary Excel workbook.
tools.when: Broad read-only documentation of an environment for audit reports; runs as an ordinary domain user and works from non-member hosts over LDAP.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/adrecon/ADRecon && .\ADRecon.ps1 on a Windows host

tools.name: AD-Audit
tools.desc: Modular PowerShell auditing suite aligned to Microsoft security best practices: user/computer hygiene, group policy, domain-controller security, credential-theft prevention, least privilege, AD FS, event monitoring, and ADCS checks with SQLite-backed findings.
tools.when: Teams wanting an extensible, automation-friendly policy-check audit (CI/CD output) rather than a single maturity score.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/adrian207/AD-Audit && Import-Module .\AD-Audit.psd1 (requires PowerShell 5.1+ and the RSAT ActiveDirectory module)

domains.name: Binary Exploitation & Reverse Engineering
domains.tagline: Debug, disassemble, decompile, and understand binaries — your own code, lab targets, and CTF challenges.

tools.name: GDB
tools.desc: The GNU Debugger — breakpoints, watchpoints, register/memory inspection, and scripting for any ELF or Mach-O binary you control.
tools.when: The backbone of all dynamic work here; run it plain for a minimal setup or host pwndbg/GEF on top of it.

tools.name: pwndbg
tools.desc: GDB plugin adding exploit-focused conveniences: heap/stack/register views, ROP-gadget search, cyclic pattern generation, and prettier disassembly.
tools.when: Drop it into GDB for CTF pwn challenges or when reversing a binary you own, to spot useful gadgets and mitigations instantly.

tools.name: GEF
tools.desc: Standalone, dependency-light GDB plugin (a single script) with heap visualizations, format-string helpers, and live memory introspection.
tools.when: Want the pwndbg-style workflow with zero setup beyond one curl command, on any GDB build.

tools.name: LLDB
tools.desc: LLVM's debugger, well integrated with Mach-O binaries, clang-generated debug info, and Swift/Objective-C symbols.
tools.when: Analyzing Apple-platform binaries or anything built with the LLVM toolchain where GDB support lags.

tools.name: Frida
tools.desc: Dynamic instrumentation toolkit that injects JavaScript into a running process (yours or a lab/CTF target) to hook functions and read live memory without recompiling.
tools.when: Trace calls, intercept functions, or inspect a live process dynamically — especially on targets where GDB struggles.

tools.name: Ghidra
tools.desc: NSA's free reverse-engineering suite with a GUI and a real decompiler that emits C-like pseudocode from machine code, plus a scriptable API.
tools.when: Full static analysis of a binary you own or a CTF challenge — the decompiler output reads far closer to source than raw disassembly.
tools.install: Download the current release zip from the GitHub releases page, unzip, and run ./ghidraRun

tools.name: radare2
tools.desc: Command-line reverse-engineering framework with an analyzer, disassembler, and ESIL emulation, scriptable via r2pipe.
tools.when: Headless or scripted analysis, quick on-box triage, and when everything should live in one terminal tool.

tools.name: rizin
tools.desc: Community fork of radare2 aiming for a cleaner, better-tested codebase while staying command-compatible and offering rz-pipe scripting and Rust bindings.
tools.when: Same CLI workflow as radare2 when you prefer the actively focused fork or need its language bindings.

tools.name: Cutter
tools.desc: Qt GUI front-end for the Rizin reversing engine giving point-and-click disassembly, patching, and analysis in a visual workspace.
tools.when: Visual exploration and annotation of binaries without a terminal-heavy workflow.

tools.name: pwntools
tools.desc: CTF pwn toolkit providing packing (p64/u64), ELF parsing, cyclic patterns, ROP-chain builders, and managed local/remote I/O for exploit prototyping.
tools.when: Prototype and test exploit behavior against binaries in a lab or CTF; the standard glue for the whole workflow.

tools.name: angr
tools.desc: Python binary analysis framework using symbolic/concolic execution to explore paths and solve constraints against a binary you control.
tools.when: Automated pathfinding — such as deriving inputs that satisfy checks — when manual reversing is too slow.

tools.name: Ropper
tools.desc: Python tool that inventories ROP gadgets and builds chains from ELF, PE, and Mach-O binaries; also powers the ROP search inside pwndbg.
tools.when: Quick gadget inventory of a binary in a lab to audit what sequences are constructible.

tools.name: one_gadget
tools.desc: Matches libc builds to single-address execve('/bin/sh') gadgets whose register constraints are simple to satisfy.
tools.when: You have a libc build in a lab or CTF and want short candidate gadget addresses before scripting the constraints.

tools.name: checksec
tools.desc: Bash/Python script that reads ELF headers and reports the active mitigations: PIE, NX, canaries, RELRO, Fortify, and more.
tools.when: First move on any binary in a lab or CTF — establish the mitigation baseline before choosing deeper tooling.

tools.name: file
tools.desc: Identifies a file's type by reading magic bytes and headers, including the format and target architecture (e.g. ELF 64-bit x86-64).
tools.when: Instant triage of any unknown artifact to confirm what you are looking at before deeper analysis.

tools.name: strings
tools.desc: Prints printable character sequences from a binary, exposing embedded literals, format strings, and library references without executing it.
tools.when: Grab a quick inventory of interesting strings — prompts, /bin/sh, format specifiers — before disassembling.

tools.name: objdump/readelf
tools.desc: binutils disassembler and ELF reader: symbol tables, sections, headers, dynamic imports, and per-arch disassembly of your own binaries.
tools.when: Zero-dependency static lookups — grep symbols, inspect section layout, or dump disassembly without a full RE suite.

tools.name: xorsearch
tools.desc: Finds payloads XORed with single-byte or multi-byte keys by matching against known plaintext strings inside packed or obfuscated binaries.
tools.when: Spot obfuscated strings or embedded shellcode in a lab binary — like strings, but for the XOR layer.

domains.name: Command & Control Frameworks
domains.tagline: C2 / post-exploitation frameworks, implants, and tunnel helpers — for authorized adversary simulation, C2-traffic detection testing, and lab post-exploitation.

tools.name: Sliver
tools.desc: Open-source cross-platform adversary-emulation framework (BishopFox); Go implants are dynamically compiled with per-binary encryption keys and support C2 over mTLS, WireGuard, HTTP(S), and DNS.
tools.when: Your default lab/red-team C2 when you want a framework blue teams can profile exhaustively without commercial licensing.

tools.name: Havoc
tools.desc: Modern malleable post-exploitation framework pairing a Qt client with a Go teamserver; the Demon agent speaks AES-encrypted HTTP(S)/SMB and uses indirect syscalls. Maintenance stopped — repo archived Feb 2026 — yet it stays a heavily studied, MITRE-tracked (S1229) traffic class.
tools.when: Lab and detection research against a well-documented post-exploitation stack (tunnel, AMSI/ETW patching, BOF/COFF loading) whose artifacts most EDRs now fingerprint.

tools.name: Mythic
tools.desc: Collaborative, Docker-based post-exploitation platform whose core ships no agents; you install agent payload types (Apollo/.NET, Athena/Rust, and others) and C2 profiles as separate containers via mythic-cli and the Mythic scripting API.
tools.when: Long-running lab engagements needing a pluggable, community-vetted agent ecosystem, cross-team collaboration, and GraphQL/automation hooks for red-team reporting.

tools.name: Merlin
tools.desc: Go-based post-exploitation server/agent pair communicating over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, h2c, and HTTP/3 (QUIC) — a practical model for non-TLS and modern protocol beaconing.
tools.when: Lab tests of HTTP/2 and QUIC transport detection, since most defensive tuning focuses on plain HTTPS beacon patterns.

tools.name: Covenant
tools.desc: Collaborative .NET C2 with a browser UI whose Grunt implants are dynamically compiled C# — the canonical worked example of .NET post-exploitation patterns (in-memory loading, AMSI/ETW patching, SMB P2P). Effectively unmaintained since ~2021 (last push 2024); now a lab/museum reference and signature-rich detection target.
tools.when: Studying .NET post-exploitation design and beating on well-known signatures in the lab; treat it as a legacy framework, not for live operations.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/cobbr/Covenant && cd Covenant/Covenant && dotnet build -c Release

tools.name: Villain
tools.desc: High-level stage 0/1 C2 handler for many reverse-TCP and HoaxShell (HTTPS) shells, shipped with Windows/Linux payload templates, fileless scripting, and cross-instance session sharing.
tools.when: Quick-sided Kali lab work that needs concurrent shell handling and payload-template experimentation without standing up a full framework.

tools.name: Cobalt Strike
tools.desc: Commercial threat-emulation platform (Fortra) and the de-facto reference C2; Malleable C2 profiles reshape HTTP(S)/DNS beacon traffic into the traffic shapes blue teams tune their detections around. Vetted licensing only: new licenses roughly $3.5k–$10k/user/yr, with cracked builds aggressively taken down.
tools.when: When you are an authorized red team that can buy it, or to study the beacon patterns that dominate C2 detection research.

tools.name: Brute Ratel C4
tools.desc: Commercial evasion-first C2 (Dark Vortex) built around the Badger implant and Commander UI, with EDR-bypass techniques (sleep obfuscation, hook removal) and a custom compiler introduced in v2.3 'Flux'. Single-user one-year license ~$3250; authorized owners only.
tools.when: Stress-testing EDR detections against an evasion-focused implant in your licensed lab; build a Brute Ratel detection story before it is needed in an incident.

tools.name: Nighthawk
tools.desc: Commercial C2 from MDSec's ActiveBreach team engineered for high-assurance detection evasion, with per-build watermarking (builds are attributable) and online-activated, hardware-locked licensing. ~$10k/user/yr, minimum three seats, UK export-controlled and vendor-vetted.
tools.when: Budgeted, mature red teams that can meet its vetting and seat minimum; otherwise, its published tradecraft makes a documented benchmark for hardening detector coverage.

tools.name: CrossC2
tools.desc: Extension that generates cross-platform beacons for Cobalt Strike (Linux, macOS, Android/ARM, even ESXi) from a configured HTTPS listener, via genCrossC2 plus automatic Malleable C2 profile handling.
tools.when: Extending a Cobalt Strike lab to authorized non-Windows assets where stock Beacon cannot run, or studying cross-platform beacon metadata.
tools.install: Download genCrossC2 + CrossC2.cna from the GitHub release

tools.name: Donut
tools.desc: Generates position-independent shellcode that stages .NET assemblies, PE files, and VBS/JScript entirely in memory, so a lab agent can be delivered without touching disk on the test host.
tools.when: Producing an in-memory delivery stage for a lab agent and observing how loaders that patch AMSI/ETW look from a defender's perspective.

tools.name: Ligolo-ng
tools.desc: Tunneling/pivoting tool that exposes a TUN interface and routes TCP/UDP through an agent over reverse TCP/TLS, reaching remote lab subnets without SOCKS/proxychains, with a web UI and autoroute since v0.8.
tools.when: Reaching the rest of an authorized test network from a C2 foothold — pivot activity blue teams should recognize and alert on.
tools.install: Download proxy & agent binaries from GitHub releases

tools.name: Chisel
tools.desc: Single-binary fast TCP/UDP tunnel carried over HTTP(S)/WebSocket (SSH-secured) with reverse port-forwarding and SOCKS — communication that reads as ordinary WebSocket/web traffic to defenders.
tools.when: Bridging egress-filtered lab segments to your C2, or tunnelling any service where the traffic should blend with normal HTTPS.

domains.name: Cryptography Toolkit & Cryptoanalysis
domains.tagline: Decode/encode data, identify encodings, and break weak ciphers and RSA on materials you own: CTF crypto, historical ciphers, and flawed implementations. Password recovery lives in 'passwords'.

tools.name: CyberChef
tools.desc: GCHQ's browser 'Cyber Swiss Army Knife': 480+ chainable operations for decoding/encoding (Base64, hex, URL, Rot13), hashing, XOR and compression, plus the Magic operation that auto-detects and unwraps multi-layer encodings. Entirely client-side, zero install.
tools.when: First stop for any blob, hex dump or encoded string: click the Magic icon to auto-decode, then drag operations to peel off the layers you identify.

tools.name: CyberChef (self-hosted)
tools.desc: The same GCHQ app run from the official pre-built Docker image (or a downloadable static build) so every operation executes inside your own network with no outbound traffic.
tools.when: Offline, air-gapped or VM work where the input must never leave your machine - identical recipes and Magic, no internet dependency after the image pull.

tools.name: xortool
tools.desc: Python tool for multi-byte XOR cipher analysis: guesses key length via equality-based scoring, recovers key bytes from the most frequent plaintext character, with charset filtering and known-plaintext (-p) options to confirm candidates.
tools.when: Ciphertext is XOR-encoded with an unknown repeating key - feed the raw bytes, let it rank key lengths, then solve for the right length and character.

tools.name: hash_extender
tools.desc: Ron Bowes' C tool for the hash length-extension attack on MD4/MD5/RIPEMD-160/SHA-0/SHA-1/SHA-256/SHA-512/Whirlpool: given a secret-prefix hash, forges a valid hash for appended data without knowing the secret, iterating guessed secret lengths.
tools.when: A service signs 'secret || message' with a Merkle-Damgård hash (CTF or your own app) and you can control appended data - produce the new payload+signature pair the server accepts.

tools.name: CrypTool
tools.desc: Legacy university/open-source cryptology suite (CrypTool 2.1 + JCrypTool) for experimenting with classical ciphers (Caesar, Vigenère, Enigma, ADFGVX) and their built-in automated cryptanalysis on paste-in text.
tools.when: Interactive analysis of historical substitution/transposition ciphers or learning the attack against a classical scheme on your own text, where a GUI beats hand-rolled scripts.

tools.name: RsaCtfTool
tools.desc: Python RSA multi-attack harness (60+ attacks): weak-key factorization (Fermat, Pollard rho, ECM, SIQS), lattice attacks on small d (Wiener, Boneh-Durfee), Hastad broadcast, shared-factor pools, ROCA, past-CTF/gimmick primes and Factordb integration; recovers the private key and/or decrypts files.
tools.when: Given a weak RSA public key and ciphertext (CTF, lab, keys you own) without knowing the weakness - run the default attack set, then target the specific winning attack.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/RsaCtfTool/RsaCtfTool && cd RsaCtfTool && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Factordb
tools.desc: Online database of integer factorizations with a plain API (https://factordb.com/api?query=N) that returns a number's status (FF/C/PRP) and known factors, including factorized prime records.
tools.when: A modulus (or any big integer) may already be factored in the public corpus - script the API from curl; RsaCtfTool queries it automatically via --attack factordb.

tools.name: rsatool
tools.desc: Small Python tool that reconstructs the full RSA key set (n, e, d, p, q, CRT params) and writes an OpenSSL-compatible PEM/DER private key from just (p, q) or (n, d), including n+dp-based factoring.
tools.when: After any attack yields p and q (or n+d): turn recovered parameters into a real private key file you can decrypt with, instead of rolling the CRT math by hand.
tools.install: wget -O rsatool.py https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ius/rsatool/master/rsatool.py && pip3 install gmpy2 pyasn1

tools.name: OpenSSL
tools.desc: The de-facto CLI crypto Swiss-army knife: AES/ChaCha20/RSA/ECDSA encryption and decryption, key generation and parsing (PEM/DER), X.509 cert/genrsa/inspect, digests, and CMS/PKCS#7 envelopes in one command.
tools.when: Quick symmetric or asymmetric encrypt/decrypt of your files, dumping or inspecting keys and certificates, and validating algorithm behavior against a standards reference implementation.

tools.name: GnuPG
tools.desc: GNU Privacy Guard: full OpenPGP implementation for asymmetric and symmetric encryption, signing/verification, keyring management, and export/import interop with PGP e-mail workflows.
tools.when: Working with .gpg/PGP messages or OpenPGP keys where the PGP container format - not raw OpenSSL cipher - is expected.

tools.name: age
tools.desc: Simple, modern, audited file encryption (X25519, optional passphrase; hybrid post-quantum ML-KEM-768 since v1.3) with small explicit keys, no configuration and UNIX-style composability; interoperable Rust port is 'rage'.
tools.when: Modern default for encrypting archives/files you own end-to-end (backups, secrets transfer) when you want minimal friction and small keys over legacy OpenPGP keyrings.

tools.name: GnuTLS certtool
tools.desc: CLI from the GnuTLS project for X.509 certificate/key generation, PKCS#12 bundles, certificate and private-key inspection, and PKCS#11 token operations through a single binary.
tools.when: Generating or inspecting certificates and PKCS#12 files with readable options, or poking at PKCS#11 tokens, when OpenSSL's flag surface gets in the way.

domains.name: Exploitation & Payload Generation
domains.tagline: Build, source, and deliver exploits and payloads against systems you own or are authorized to test.

tools.name: Metasploit Framework
tools.desc: Modular exploitation toolkit that packages exploit modules, payloads, encoders, and post-exploitation into one console on Kali.
tools.when: Your first stop when a known CVE has a module: select the target, pick the module, review the options, and run it against your lab host.

tools.name: BeEF
tools.desc: Browser Exploitation Framework that hooks a browser via a small JavaScript and then commands it through a web UI.
tools.when: Client-side testing where the goal is to exercise browser-based controls (cookies, XSS) in a browser you control.

tools.name: RouterSploit
tools.desc: Python framework for embedded-device exploits (routers, cameras, and other IoT gear) with a searchable module tree.
tools.when: Vulnerability-testing firmware on routers you own; pairs with the hardware-hacking firmware image tooling in this repo.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/threat9/routersploit && cd routersploit && python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: msfvenom
tools.desc: Shellcode and payload generator included with Metasploit, producing single payloads from a huge format/architecture matrix.
tools.when: Produce a reverse shell or staged payload for a specific OS/arch, then serve it wet and dry via your listener during authorized tests.

tools.name: PayloadsAllTheThings
tools.desc: Curated repository of webapp, injection, and reverse-shell payloads organized by vulnerability class.
tools.when: Copy the right payload shape for injection/deserialization cases instead of hand-writing it from memory during a pentest.

tools.name: SearchSploit
tools.desc: Offline command-line search into a local copy of the Exploit-DB archive, filtering by platform and port.
tools.when: Search for public PoCs before touching a CVE; works air-gapped on a Kali box with no internet.

tools.name: Exploit-DB (web)
tools.desc: The web interface to the same archive, adding full-text search, verified PoCs, and paper writeups.
tools.when: Browse recent additions and read the writeup behind a PoC when the offline search gives you just a filename.

tools.name: NVD
tools.desc: NIST vulnerability database that pins down CVSS scores, CPE identifiers, and affected-version ranges per CVE.
tools.when: Confirm version-to-CVE mappings and exploitability metrics before you go hunting for a specific PoC.

tools.name: socat
tools.desc: Bidirectional data relay that spoofs source IPs, adds TLS, and can chain listeners, making raw TCP/UDP shells robust.
tools.when: Stand up the listener that receives an outbound shell, and the second listener that relays it reliably, for your own test hosts.

tools.name: netcat / ncat
tools.desc: Classic TCP/UDP Swiss-army tool where one host listens on a port and the other pipes in/out; ncat is the modern Nmap build.
tools.when: The quickest minimal listener, or when you need ncat's extra features (SSL, send-only, proxy) on a box that only has netcat.

tools.name: RevShells
tools.desc: Web generator that prints ready-made reverse-shell one-liners for many languages (bash, netcat, powershell, python, socat).
tools.when: Copy a correctly-encoded payload for a specific listener IP/port instead of re-memorizing one-liner syntax.

tools.name: sbd
tools.desc: Netcat-style tool with AES-128 encrypted connections and multi-connection waiting, bundled in Kali.
tools.when: Whip up an encrypted shell listener/client pair on test infrastructure so the traffic isn't plaintext over the wire.

tools.name: pwntools
tools.desc: Python library for writing exploit scripts: assembles shellcode, manages processes/sockets, and packs/unpacks addresses cleanly.
tools.when: Write a repeatable exploit script (buffer overflow, format string) with assembly and encoding helpers under your own rooftop test process.

tools.name: pwndbg
tools.desc: GDB-embedded plugin that formats registers, stack, and hexdumps at every breakpoint so binary exploitation is readable.
tools.when: Debug a crash payload instruction-by-instruction in a local, vetted binary when a plain gdb layout is too noisy.

tools.name: ROPgadget
tools.desc: Scans binaries for return-oriented programming gadgets (and can dump the full gadget set or specific instructions).
tools.when: Collect usable ROP gadgets from a stripped binary of your own target before assembling a chain.

tools.name: GDB
tools.desc: The GNU debugger: sets breakpoints, examines memory, and single-steps program execution on the system being tested.
tools.when: Trace exactly where a test payload corrupts state in a process you are allowed to debug on the local machine.

domains.name: IoT, Embedded & Firmware Security
domains.tagline: Reverse, emulate, and attack embedded devices in your lab: firmware extraction, boot-level emulation, JTAG/UART probing, side-channels, and RFID.

tools.name: binwalk
tools.desc: Identifies and extracts embedded files and filesystems (squashfs, cramfs, JFFS2, kernels, U-Boot) from a firmware image via magic signatures, with entropy analysis to find encrypted/compressed regions.
tools.when: Every firmware image starts here: carve the filesystem out of the blob before anything else can run.

tools.name: FirmWalker
tools.desc: Bash script that greps an extracted or mounted root filesystem for secrets: etc/shadow and passwd, SSL keys/certs, config files, admin/password keywords, dropbear/ssh, and URLs.
tools.when: Ten seconds after binwalk extraction to surface default creds, key material, and backdoors before you read anything by hand.

tools.name: firmware-mod-kit (FMK)
tools.desc: Extract-and-rebuild toolkit for router firmware (squashfs/cramfs/JFFS2); lets you patch binaries or files and repack a bootable image. Legacy: descended from the Google Code project and largely unmaintained, so expect to fix toolchain issues.
tools.when: When you actually need to modify and re-flash a vendor image (e.g. inject a telnetd) rather than just read it.

tools.name: QEMU
tools.desc: Full-system emulator covering ARM, MIPS, RISC-V, and more; boots extracted Linux root filesystems or bare-metal board images, and its user-mode builds runs single binaries or architectures different to your host.
tools.when: The foundation for all emulation: boot the extracted filesystem, or dynamically analyze a single firmware binary before wiring up full-stack tooling.

tools.name: FirmAE
tools.desc: Fully-automated emulation framework (Firmadyne-derived) that uses arbitration heuristics to boot router/IP-camera firmware at ~79% success, exposing the web UI/SSH so you can fuzz and exploit it dynamically.
tools.when: Full-system dynamic analysis of Linux-based IoT firmware on a big batch, when Firmadyne-style boot failures are blocking you.

tools.name: Firmware Analysis Toolkit (FAT)
tools.desc: Attify's one-command wrapper around Firmadyne that boots Linux router firmware in QEMU without the PostgreSQL dependency; prints the emulated IP so you can hit its web server from the host.
tools.when: Quick, scripted boot of a single firmware image to reach its web UI and poke at it by hand.

tools.name: OpenOCD
tools.desc: On-chip debugger for JTAG/SWD with a large catalog of CPU and flash targets, dozens of adapter drivers, and scripting via TCL; reads flash dumps, halts CPUs, and sets breakpoints on running firmware.
tools.when: You found a JTAG/SWD header (or pin out a testpad): OpenOCD + a cheap adapter gets you a debugger on nearly any target.

tools.name: urJTAG
tools.desc: Universal JTAG library and tools, descendant of the old openwince tools; strong at boundary-scan and flash programming where OpenOCD lacks target or chain support.
tools.when: JTAG chains, boundary scan over infrastructure, or obscure flash parts that OpenOCD doesn't have configured.

tools.name: Bus Pirate
tools.desc: Open-source serial multi-tool (Bus Pirate 5 current): drive SPI/I2C/UART/1-Wire, read serial flash and EEPROMs, sniff buses, act as a low-speed logic analyzer, and glitch a target — all from a serial terminal.
tools.when: Dumping an SPI flash or EEPROM, sniffing an I2C/SPI bus between chips, or quick protocol probing before you break out a full logic analyzer.
tools.install: hardware (dangerousprototypes.com) + any serial terminal, e.g. sudo apt install picocom

tools.name: minicom
tools.desc: The classic serial terminal for UART consoles at arbitrary baud rates; the everyday tool for reaching a bootloader, root shell, or firmware upgrade prompt over the debug UART.
tools.when: UART pads/traces are exposed and you want bootloader or shell access to the device quickly.

tools.name: J-Link (SEGGER)
tools.desc: Commercial debug-probe family (SEGGER) with polished SWD/JTAG software, flash loader support across thousands of micros, and RTT for fast printf-style logging from target firmware.
tools.when: A board already exposes a J-Link/SWD header, or you want a trouble-free flash-and-debug flow on a supported MCU instead of fighting adapter quirks.
tools.install: commercial hardware + SEGGER J-Link software suite (segger.com)

tools.name: ChipWhisperer
tools.desc: Open-source, open-hardware lab for power/EM side-channel analysis and voltage/clock glitching: capture power traces, run correlation power analysis to recover keys, and glitch to skip checks (CW-Lite, CW-Husky).
tools.when: Assessing a secure MCU's resistance to key extraction or fault injection — on a target board you own — where the hardware is the oracle.

tools.name: Proxmark3
tools.desc: The Swiss-army RFID/NFC research device (125 kHz + 13.56 MHz) covering low- and high-frequency tags — Mifare, iClass, HID, ISO14443/ISO15693, EMV — to sniff, clone, and pen-test access credentials; use the actively maintained Iceman firmware fork.
tools.when: Reading, sniffing, or cloning badges, keyfobs, and access-control cards you legitimately test, plus auditing a site's RFID exposure.

tools.name: libnfc
tools.desc: Low-level NFC library with CLI tools (nfc-list, nfc-mfclassic, nfclibnfc) that read, write, and clone ISO14443A tags through cheap USB readers like the ACR122U.
tools.when: Quick reads (UID, Mifare classic blocks) with a plain USB NFC reader before you reach for a full Proxmark3.

domains.name: Mobile Application Security (Android & iOS)
domains.tagline: Testing your own or authorized Android & iOS apps: static analysis, decompilation, runtime instrumentation, traffic interception, and attack-surface automation.

tools.name: MobSF (Mobile Security Framework)
tools.desc: Automated all-in-one analyzer for APK, IPA, and Windows mobile binaries: permissions, exported components, insecure manifest/crypto config, hardcoded secrets, and OWASP MASTG-style checks surfaced in a clean web UI plus REST API for CI.
tools.when: Always the first pass on an app binary you are authorized to test — upload the APK or IPA, read the findings report, then drill into specific hits for manual follow-up.

tools.name: Quark-Engine
tools.desc: Obfuscation-neglect APK scoring engine (distinct from the old LinkedIn 'qark'): matches the app's call graph against a rule set of suspicious behaviors — crypto misuse, dynamic dex loading, accessibility/SMS abuse, C2 calls — and emits confidence-scored reports.
tools.when: Quick second opinion on an APK for risky behavior patterns after MobSF, or to generate new detection rules from code you reverse yourself.

tools.name: APKiD
tools.desc: YARA-based detector for packers, protectors, and obfuscators (DexProtector, Bangcle, qihoo, etc.) inside an APK/DEX before any reversing effort begins.
tools.when: Scope a hardened app early: knowing it is packed tells you static-only analysis is not enough and you will need runtime dexdump (frida-dexdump).

tools.name: jadx
tools.desc: One-step DEX-to-Java decompiler with GUI and CLI that rebuilds readable Java source, resources, and AndroidManifest.xml into a searchable whole-project view.
tools.when: Default decompilation of a fresh APK: navigate the reconstructed project, follow flows across classes, and copy logic into notes.
tools.install: Download the latest zip from GitHub releases (or 'brew install jadx')

tools.name: apktool
tools.desc: Decodes Android resources and AndroidManifest.xml into editable form and rebuilds the APK; exposes smali/baksmali bytecode for patching when Java source is not needed.
tools.when: Modify res/ or smali and repackage the APK (behavior/repackage tests), or pull the manifest cleanly when jadx output gets mangled.
tools.install: Download the jar wrapper from GitHub releases (or 'sudo apt install apktool')

tools.name: frida-dexdump
tools.desc: Dumps in-memory DEX files from a running app via Frida, defeating packers and protectors that only materialize code at runtime.
tools.when: Analyze a packed/hardened app: launch it on a device, dump the loaded dex at runtime, then feed the recovered classes back into jadx.

tools.name: dex2jar
tools.desc: The classic DEX-to-JAR converter (paired with JD-GUI for a quick Java view); effectively unmaintained but still the format older guides and toolchains expect.
tools.when: Legacy fallback decompile when jadx chokes on an unusual format, or when a downstream tooling chain requires .jar/.class input.

tools.name: Frida
tools.desc: Cross-platform dynamic instrumentation toolkit: inject a frida-server process onto Android/iOS to hook functions, bypass SSL pinning and root detection, trace crypto calls, and invoke internal methods from a Python/JS REPL.
tools.when: The runtime layer of most mobile tests — bypass cert pinning, trace sensitive functions, dump buffers, and poke internals static analysis cannot reach.
tools.install: pip install frida-tools && push a matching-version frida-server to the device

tools.name: objection
tools.desc: Frida-powered runtime exploration toolkit: one-liners to disable SSL pinning and root checks, browse Android/iOS storage (Keychain, SharedPrefs, Bundle), and explore exported classes without writing custom JS.
tools.when: Quick interactive runtime pass on your own app — disable pinning/root detection and inspect stored data — when hand-writing Frida scripts is overkill.

tools.name: Magisk
tools.desc: Systemless rooting framework for physical Android devices and emulators that gives Frida, adb, and your injected agents the root context most dynamic tests need; it is a rooting kit first, not a pentest tool.
tools.when: Prepare a dedicated test device with an unlocked bootloader when an app refuses to run on stock or detects the emulator you were using.
tools.install: Install the Magisk APK or 'fastboot boot magisk_patched-<hash>.img' on an unlocked-bootloader device

tools.name: adb (Android Debug Bridge)
tools.desc: Google's core device bridge from Android platform-tools: install apps, push/pull files, shell in, port-forward, install CA certificates, and capture logcat.
tools.when: Every device setup step — enumerate devices, push frida-server and test certificates, and snapshot app data before and after a test run.

tools.name: mitmproxy
tools.desc: Interactive HTTPS intercepting proxy built for mobile workflows: install its CA on the device, replay or rewrite HTTP/2 and gRPC flows, and script custom handling with Python addons; pair with a Frida/objection pinning bypass to decrypt app TLS.
tools.when: Any network-level test of your own apps — log, tamper, or replay API traffic from a rooted device, emulator, or iOS simulator.

tools.name: Charles Proxy
tools.desc: Commercial GUI HTTPS proxy with click-through SSL proxying, rewrite/breakpoints, and a visual request timeline — the macOS-centric alternative to a terminal proxy.
tools.when: Point-and-click interception and rewriting during manual iOS testing on a workstation when you prefer a GUI over mitmproxy's keyboard-driven flow.
tools.install: Download from charlesproxy.com (trial, then paid license)

tools.name: Drozer
tools.desc: The reference Android attack-surface framework: an on-device agent lets you assume the role of another app and enumerate/exploit exported activities, content providers, services, and broadcast receivers from a console.
tools.when: After static analysis, map the app's IPC/component attack surface and probe each exported component for authorization and data-exposure flaws.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ReversecLabs/drozer.git && cd drozer && pip install . (plus the drozer agent APK on the device)

tools.name: Android Tamer
tools.desc: Linux distro/VM prebundling dozens of Android-sec tools (jadx, apktool, MobSF, AndroBugs, Frida, radare2). Tamer 4 is end-of-life and Tamer 5 is under construction, so it is a convenience starting point, not a project to build on.
tools.when: Stand up a one-shot preconfigured Android-tools VM for a specific engagement; otherwise skip — each tool here installs more reliably on your own base OS.
tools.install: Download the Tamer 4 VM from TamerPlatform and import into VirtualBox/VMware

tools.name: Frida-iOS
tools.desc: Frida on iOS for hooking, swizzling, and runtime inspection of app classes on jailbroken devices.
tools.when: When you need to trace iOS app runtime behavior on jailbroken devices.

tools.name: Frida-codeshare
tools.desc: Collection of iOS-focused Frida scripts for class dumping and method tracing.
tools.when: Need common iOS hooks without writing your own.

domains.name: Network Attacks & Analysis
domains.tagline: Packet capture, on-path interception, host discovery, and connectivity utilities for understanding and testing traffic on networks you operate.

tools.name: Wireshark
tools.desc: Graphical packet analyzer that decodes hundreds of protocols, follows TCP streams, and reassembles sessions live or from a saved capture.
tools.when: See the actual bytes and protocol conversations behind a traffic sample, or replay an issue from a .pcap taken on a machine you control.

tools.name: tcpdump
tools.desc: Command-line packet capture using Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) expressions; the standard for headless logging and scripted sniffing.
tools.when: On servers, routers, or lab hosts where no GUI exists, or when writing a rolling capture to a file for later analysis.

tools.name: tshark
tools.desc: Wireshark's terminal sibling: captures, decrypts, and prints live or offline traffic with the full dissector set and CSV/JSON output.
tools.when: Get Wireshark-grade dissection piped into grep, awk, or analysis scripts without launching a GUI.

tools.name: tcpflow
tools.desc: Reassembles TCP sessions from a capture into separate per-connection files, ignoring lower-level packet noise.
tools.when: Reconstruct actual transferred content (files, HTTP bodies) from a .pcap you own instead of inspecting packets one at a time.

tools.name: bettercap
tools.desc: Modular framework for MITM, ARP/DNS/DHCP spoofing, and credential sniffing with an interactive shell and RESTful API for scripting.
tools.when: On a network you operate, to test which plaintext protocols (HTTP, FTP, telnet) leak over the wire and how clients react to spoofing.

tools.name: mitmproxy
tools.desc: Interactive HTTPS interception proxy with a terminal UI, Python addon scripting, and TLS interception via its own CA you install on your devices.
tools.when: Inspect and rewrite HTTP/HTTPS traffic from an app, device, or CLI you control, with the proxy cert explicitly trusted on that device.

tools.name: responder
tools.desc: Answers LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS name-resolution queries on a subnet and logs or relays credentials passed over those protocols to its own listeners.
tools.when: Test Windows-style authentication flows in a lab and check whether clients will send net-NTLM hashes when their expected resolver goes silent.

tools.name: arp-scan
tools.desc: Sends ARP requests to every address in a subnet and lists live hosts by IP and MAC/OUI vendor; the most reliable way to map a local network.
tools.when: First step when on a network you administer: enumerate every physical host on the LAN, since ARP is answered even where ICMP is filtered.

tools.name: netdiscover
tools.desc: Active and passive ARP-based host discovery with a live-updating table of MAC address, vendor, and IP.
tools.when: Continuous visual recon of a local network, or a quick live view while monitoring the LAN over time.

tools.name: fping
tools.desc: Bulk ICMP pinger that sweeps a range of targets in parallel and prints alive/dead results in a script-friendly stream.
tools.when: Fast liveness check of a large IP range when hosts are off-subnet, where ARP-based discovery cannot reach.

tools.name: socat
tools.desc: Bidirectional relay that forwards, listens on, and connects across TCP, UDP, UNIX sockets, and files; flexible byte plumbing for testing services.
tools.when: Expose a local service through a relay, forward ports between lab hosts, or inject/monitor raw data flows in ad-hoc setups.

tools.name: ncat
tools.desc: Nmap's free, MIT-licensed netcat: connect, listen, and relay TCP/UDP with TLS, proxy modes, and easy scripting built in.
tools.when: Quick read/write tests against a listening port, banner grabbing, or one-shot TCP/UDP checks while debugging connectivity.

tools.name: hping3
tools.desc: Packet-crafting tool that builds custom TCP/UDP/ICMP packets via raw sockets, with control over flags, timing, and fragmentation.
tools.when: Answer questions like "does this firewall actually drop that flagged packet?" by sending hand-crafted probes from a host you control.

tools.name: proxychains
tools.desc: Routes any TCP client through a strict, random, or dynamic chain of HTTP/SOCKS proxies, forcing connections out via chosen exits.
tools.when: Test whether an application can be tunneled through proxies and observe the egress path a tool takes in controlled lab scenarios.

tools.name: dig
tools.desc: The standard DNS query tool from the BIND suite: any record type, MX priority, zone-transfer attempts, and query tracing against a chosen resolver.
tools.when: Resolve names in isolation, verify records against a specific server, or trace how a lookup flows through resolvers in one command.

tools.name: whois
tools.desc: Queries WHOIS/registration databases for domain ownership, registrar, name servers, and IP allocation details.
tools.when: Collect registrant, registrar, and registration dates for a domain, or the owning organization of an IP range, before deeper analysis.

domains.name: OSINT — People, Infrastructure & Metadata
domains.tagline: Passive intelligence on people, exposed infrastructure, and document metadata — for authorized recon and for auditing your own digital footprint.

tools.name: Sherlock
tools.desc: Checks a username across 400+ social networks using HTTP status/pattern heuristics; the most widely maintained CLI for username existence.
tools.when: Find every public profile tied to a username you own, or verify a handle before cleaning up your own exposure.

tools.name: Maigret
tools.desc: Collects a username dossier across 3000+ sites, tagging each account by type (social, dating, code) and generating HTML/PDF/JSON reports; actively maintained with a frequently refreshed site database.
tools.when: When Sherlock's pass/fail list is not enough and you want account tags, graph export, and a readable report of where a username appears.

tools.name: WhatsMyName
tools.desc: A community-maintained JSON dataset covering 700+ sites with exact success/not-found detections; the data layer behind many username checkers and the whatsmyname.app web UI since the bundled checker scripts were removed in 2023.
tools.when: When you want the raw detection data to audit a check result or drive your own checker against a curated site list.

tools.name: namechk
tools.desc: Free web service that checks a name across 100+ social platforms and 36 domain extensions in one view; a hosted service, not a self-hosted tool — no API and no bulk mode.
tools.when: A quick browser-only triage of where a name is already taken before you invest in CLI pipelines.

tools.name: theHarvester
tools.desc: Passively harvests emails, employee names, subdomains, hosts, and API leaks for a domain from open sources; the reference OSINT email/subdomain harvester, actively maintained.
tools.when: Map every email address and subdomain publicly linked to a domain you own before hardening mail and DNS.

tools.name: Holehe
tools.desc: Checks whether an email is registered on 120+ sites by replaying their password-recovery flows without sending anything to the mailbox, so the target address is not alerted.
tools.when: Find which platforms a leaked or owned email is tied to so you can spot stale accounts you control that still need securing.

tools.name: PhoneInfoga
tools.desc: Framework for phone OSINT: country, area, carrier, line type, and footprint lookups via configurable scanners; stable but no longer actively maintained, so expect scanners to drift over time.
tools.when: Resolve a phone number you own or are authorized to analyze into provider/line-type facts before deeper carrier-level checks.

tools.name: emailrep.io
tools.desc: Hosted API/service that scores an email's reputation, flags breach exposure and disposable/spammy providers, and lists the online profiles tied to it; a service, not a tool — the free tier needs no key, higher limits need one.
tools.when: Triage a suspicious inbound email or audit your own addresses for exposure as part of defensive OSINT.

tools.name: Instaloader
tools.desc: Downloads Instagram profiles, posts, hashtags, highlight stories, and companion metadata (captions, likes, comments) via its own private API without an official key; actively maintained and scriptable.
tools.when: Pull an archive of a public profile you own for media/evidence preservation, or collect hashtag and post metadata on your own accounts.

tools.name: snscrape
tools.desc: Python CLI/library that scrapes public posts and profiles from several platforms with JSONL output; Twitter/X scrapers are dead behind the login wall and Reddit needs the closed Pushshift, but Telegram, Weibo, and some Mastodon instances still work.
tools.when: Programmatic bulk retrieval and archiving of public posts from the platforms snscrape still supports, e.g. Telegram channels.

tools.name: OSINTgram
tools.desc: Interactive shell that collects public Instagram data — profile info, captions, followers, tagged users, comments, and bio contact strings — using a scratch-account session or a free HikerAPI token; the project's own disclaimer limits use to educational/authorized targets.
tools.when: Relationship analysis of a public profile you own (who comments, who is tagged, contact strings in bios).
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/Datalux/Osintgram && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Shodan
tools.desc: The reference internet device/port search engine indexing exposed services, banners, vulnerabilities, and history for any IP or domain; a commercial service with a lasting free tier and a separate no-key InternetDB lookup endpoint.
tools.when: See every port and service your public IP ranges expose right now, exactly as an attacker would, before closing them.

tools.name: Censys
tools.desc: Internet-wide scan platform covering hosts, services, certificates, and web properties with structured query language; the free tier includes search plus host/cert/web-property lookup APIs.
tools.when: Certificate-centric inventory and pivots — find every host presenting a given cert — or structured queries beyond Shodan's free tier.

tools.name: ZoomEye
tools.desc: Cyber-space search engine by KnownSec scanning IPv4/IPv6, services, and web layers via Xmap/Wmap; strongest on IoT/OT devices and Asian-region asset coverage, with roughly 10k free API queries/month.
tools.when: Coverage of less-Shodanized regions or internet-of-things/embedded device hunting on ranges you own.

tools.name: Netlas
tools.desc: Internet scanning platform over 8B+ indexed hosts with response-body, DNS, WHOIS, and certificate search plus a full REST API and Python SDK; the free tier is key-limited at about 50 requests/day.
tools.when: Regular-expression/Lucene search across full HTTP response bodies when Shodan's banners are too shallow.

tools.name: exiftool
tools.desc: Reads, writes, and edits EXIF/GPS/IPTC/XMP and hundreds of tag formats across images, PDFs, Office files, and more; the metadata workhorse behind most doc-forensics pipelines.
tools.when: Forensic-grade tag extraction from any local file — geolocation, author, generator, timestamps — before release or after acquisition.

tools.name: Metagoofil
tools.desc: Dork-driven document harvesting: finds indexed files (.pdf, .docx, .xlsx) on a domain and downloads them for stripping; the maintained opsdisk fork ships on Kali and deliberately defers metadata analysis to exiftool.
tools.when: Collect every publicly indexed document on a domain you own so you can scrub metadata and accidental information leaks.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/opsdisk/metagoofil && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: FOCA
tools.desc: Windows GUI (C# with a SQL Server back end) that searches a domain via Google/Bing/DuckDuckGo, fingerprints documents, and extracts metadata — users, folders, software — into a browsable project; a Windows GUI, not a POSIX tool, with slow updates.
tools.when: When you have a Windows box and want a point-and-click metadata project view instead of CLI pipelines.

tools.name: SpiderFoot
tools.desc: Automated OSINT correlation engine with 200+ modules and a YAML correlation engine, surfaced through a web UI and CLI; built to map an attack surface and connect entities automatically.
tools.when: A broad sweep of a domain/IP/email you own to correlate entities across many free data sources in a single scan.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/smicallef/spiderfoot && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Maltego
tools.desc: Commercial graph-based link-analysis and OSINT platform (desktop and browser) with transforms into 1B+ identities, breach data, and infrastructure datasets; a free Community Edition (Basic plan) exists but is result-limited. A commercial service, not open source.
tools.when: Investigative link analysis where a visual graph of who/what connects to whom beats JSON output.
tools.install: preinstalled (web/desktop — free CE with Maltego ID)

tools.name: recon-ng
tools.desc: Metasploit-style modular reconnaissance framework for web OSINT, with a marketplace of modules, workspace isolation, and database-backed reporting; stable but leisurely maintained.
tools.when: Scripted, repeatable recon workflows with structured output and API keys for your own estate.

tools.name: Google Hacking Database (GHDB)
tools.desc: Reference catalog of search-engine operators ('dorks') and example queries that surface exposed files, login panels, admin pages, and misconfigurations in public indexes. A reference page, not a tool.
tools.when: Compose and reuse proven search-engine queries to audit what public indexes expose about your own domains.

domains.name: Password Attacks & Cracking
domains.tagline: Offline + online cracking of hashes and logins you own: GPU/CPU recovery, wordlists, archive and file password recovery.

tools.name: Hashcat
tools.desc: World's fastest password recovery utility; GPU-optimized kernels for 590+ hash modes across dictionary (wordlist), mask/brute-force, hybrid, PCFG and rule-based attacks.
tools.when: The go-to for offline hash recovery on your own system: first benchmark, then wordlist, then mask/rule attacks. Also the home of every -a 0/3/6/7 mode and .rule files.

tools.name: hashcat-utils
tools.desc: Small MIT-licensed STDIN/STDOUT utilities (cap2hccapx, combipow, len, cutb, rulegen, …) meant to be chained into pipelines that feed hashcat candidates.
tools.when: Pre-process wordlists or extract Wi-Fi/captured hashes into the exact format hashcat needs before launching an attack.

tools.name: MaskProcessor
tools.desc: High-performance per-position word generator using hashcat-style masks (?l, ?u, ?d, ?s, ?a) and up to four custom charsets; generates candidate words hashcat guesses.
tools.when: Generate a mask-only wordlist on CPU, or build rules/masks offline before feeding them to a GPU cracking session.

tools.name: John the Ripper
tools.desc: The classic Unix password cracker: dictionary, incremental (markov), and rule-based modes, plus hundreds of hash/cipher formats in its jumbo builds; runs on CPU, GPU (OpenCL) and more.
tools.when: Default choice for /etc/shadow-style hashes and archive/doc hashes on any box, especially when GPU drivers are unavailable.

tools.name: John the Ripper jumbo
tools.desc: Community-enhanced jumbo edition (bleeding-jumbo branch): hundreds of extra formats (Windows NTLM, macOS, PDF, RAR, KeePass) and bundled *2john converters for encrypted files.
tools.when: When your hash/source file is not handled by core John or hashcat yet - the widest format coverage for offline recovery.

tools.name: ophcrack
tools.desc: Windows LM/NTLM password cracker based on rainbow tables; GUI + LiveCD, with free XP/Vista tables and SAM dumping from your own Windows installs.
tools.when: Recovering weak LM/NTLM hashes for accounts you administer, when rainbow tables beat per-hash brute forcing for short passwords.

tools.name: Hydra
tools.desc: Parallelized network login cracker supporting 50+ protocols/modules (ssh, rdp, http-get/post-form, ftp, smb, …) with -L/-P user/password lists and brute-force (-x).
tools.when: Test login strength against a live service you own (your lab router web login, your SSH server) using lists from SecLists; lowest effort-to-coverage ratio.

tools.name: Medusa
tools.desc: Thread-based modular parallel login brute-forcer (SMB, HTTP, MS-SQL, RDP, SSH, VNC and more), with combination files and host/user/password parallelism.
tools.when: When you want threaded parallel testing against multiple hosts at once and cleaner control over per-module options than Hydra gives.

tools.name: Ncrack
tools.desc: Nmap-team high-speed network authentication cracker with an Nmap-like CLI and timing templates; supports SSH, RDP, Telnet, HTTP(S), SMB, VNC, Redis and more.
tools.when: Large-scale audited hosts with an nmap-flavored mindset; note that focus has moved to the NSE brute scripts and the standalone build is 0.7 (2019).

tools.name: Patator
tools.desc: Multi-purpose flexible brute-forcer written in Python with modules for http_fuzz (web login), ssh_login, ftp_login, rdp_login and more; built to be more reliable than its predecessors.
tools.when: Web form logins and protocol guessing where you need predictable retry/ignore logic and precise module parameters.

tools.name: SecLists
tools.desc: The security tester's companion collection: passwords (10k/1M/rockyou-derived), usernames, default/router credentials, fuzzing payloads and discovery lists in one place.
tools.when: First stop in any cracking session - pull its built-in dictionaries before generating your own.

tools.name: rockyou.txt
tools.desc: The 2009 RockYou breach password list (~14M passwords, historically the free default): a solid baseline dictionary for fast-hash testing on your own targets.
tools.when: Quick first-pass dictionary attack before rule/mask work when you need a proven real-world wordlist (Kali ships it under /usr/share/wordlists).

tools.name: CeWL
tools.desc: Ruby spider that crawls a site to a depth, collects unique words (plus email/author metadata) and emits a custom wordlist for password recovery.
tools.when: Recovering passwords tied to a site's own vocabulary - e.g. your own web app or a CTF - where organization-specific words beat generic dictionaries.

tools.name: crunch
tools.desc: Wordlist generator that enumerates all combinations/permutations of a charset with pattern support (@,%^ placeholders), file-splitting, resume and gzip/7z output.
tools.when: Generate targeted candidate lists (fixed charset, known pattern positions, e.g. TailNumbers-like masks) to feed hashcat or John.

tools.name: kwprocessor
tools.desc: Advanced keyboard-walk generator that produces passwords following keyboard routes (adjacent-key walks, zxcvbn-style patterns) from configurable basechars, keymaps and route files.
tools.when: Targeting PINs/passphrases typed along keyboard patterns (your own router/phone PINs) where left-right walks are more likely than random strings.

tools.name: Mentalist
tools.desc: Graphical wordlist generator built on human password paradigms (case mangling, keyboard walks, adding years/digits); exports full wordlists or ready-made hashcat and John rules.
tools.when: Visually build a password profile (organization vocab + year + symbol) when you prefer a GUI over hand-rolling rule files.

tools.name: hashid
tools.desc: Python tool identifying 220+ hash types via regex, printing the matching hashcat mode number and John format so your next command is correct the first time.
tools.when: Immediately after collecting a hash (dump, CTF, config) - before picking -m / --format, to avoid line-length and wrong-mode failures.

tools.name: hash-identifier
tools.desc: Classic interactive script that asks candidate lines and guesses the hash algorithm family; the free counterpart hashid was written to supersede.
tools.when: A zero-dependency interactive sanity check on a single odd-looking hash when you don't have pip/Git access.

tools.name: HashCat example-hashes
tools.desc: Official reference table with one valid sample hash per hashcat mode (password is always 'hashcat'); the canonical way to confirm a hash type and test an attack command.
tools.when: Verify your command and hash formatting offline (also embedded in `hashcat --example-hashes`) before real runs, or to label samples in CTFs.

tools.name: zip2john
tools.desc: John the Ripper utility that converts encrypted ZIPs (and via siblings like rar2john, 7z2john, pdf2john) into a crackable hash for john or hashcat; fast and dependency-free.
tools.when: Recovering a forgotten password on your own ZIP/Office/PDF archive: convert first, crack with john -jumbo or hashcat after.

tools.name: fcrackzip
tools.desc: Fast zip password cracker with dictionary and brute-force modes (libzip-based fork runs ~1000x faster than the original unzip-spawning version).
tools.when: Quick direct brute/dictionary check of a single small ZIP without setting up John pipelines; keep in mind upstream notes it is largely superseded by zip2john + jumbo.

tools.name: pdfcrack
tools.desc: Small GPL tool recovering owner/user passwords from PDFs using the standard security handler (rev 2-4) via wordlist or brute force, with job save/load state.
tools.when: Recover your own locked PDF (user or owner password) when the PDF predates AES-256 rev 5; on modern AES R2/R3 PDFs prefer john's pdf2john formats.

tools.name: rarcrack
tools.desc: Brute-force password recovery for RAR, ZIP and 7Z archives with automatic resume via XML state file and thread/charset control; dormant since ~2010.
tools.when: Legacy rar3 archives only; on modern hardware and rar5 prefer rar2john + john/hashcat since rarcrack is no longer maintained.

tools.name: keepass2john
tools.desc: John jumbo converter that extracts a sealed .kdbx KeePass database into a PBKDF2/AES hash crackable by john or hashcat ($keepass$ format).
tools.when: Unlock your own KeePass vault after losing the master password - always on a copy you own, never a stored database you don't.

domains.name: Phishing & Social Engineering
domains.tagline: Simulating the human factor: phishing campaigns, cloned logins, credential harvesting, and MFA-phishing proxies — all framed for authorized security-awareness testing.

tools.name: Gophish
tools.desc: Go-based open-source phishing campaign platform: composes email templates, landing pages, target groups, and SMTP profiles, then tracks opens, clicks, and submitted credentials per recipient via web UI + REST API.
tools.when: The standard engine for organizational awareness campaigns — schedule simulations against your own employees, export per-recipient results, and measure click-rate improvement over time.

tools.name: King Phisher
tools.desc: Python client/server toolkit (SecureState) with parallel campaigns, web-page cloning, credential-harvesting landing pages, geo-location, and SPF checks. The project is declared no longer maintained — treat as legacy.
tools.when: Legacy environments or when you need a fully self-hosted client-plus-server workflow; otherwise prefer Gophish.

tools.name: SocialFish
tools.desc: Active Python toolkit for cloning modern, JavaScript-heavy login pages and reporting clicks and submissions; ships page-candidate templates useful in training demos. It also bundles cookie/OTP hooks — use only in authorized simulations against consenting participants.
tools.when: A quick page-only replica of a current login page for a live security-awareness demo without standing up a full campaign framework.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/UndeadSec/SocialFish && cd SocialFish && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Social-Engineer Toolkit (SET)
tools.desc: TrustedSec's menu-driven Python framework bundling social-engineering vectors — page cloning, credential harvesting, email mass-mailers, SMS, and more — behind one guided interface. Preinstalled on Kali and used by teams to run authorized awareness campaigns.
tools.when: Guided multi-vector campaigns on a Kali box, e.g. a quick credential-harvest or mailer exercise in-house where one menu covers everything.

tools.name: BeEF
tools.desc: Browser Exploitation Framework: serves a JavaScript hook that, once a consenting user's browser loads it, gives the operator a live inside view of that browser session with modules including fake login prompts and environment probing.
tools.when: Training where you show employees the inside of a compromised browser session live, or test whether your org detects browser-hook indicators.

tools.name: Wifiphisher
tools.desc: Rogue-access-point framework that drives nearby clients to a captive-portal page to collect Wi-Fi credentials. An authorized physical-testing and awareness tool for demonstrating Wi-Fi credential exposure on scoped, consenting networks.
tools.when: On-site assessments where the goal is showing guests/employees how easily a lookalike Wi-Fi portal harvests creds — never on networks you do not own or lack written consent for.

tools.name: Evilginx2
tools.desc: Go-based man-in-the-middle reverse proxy (authorized red-team phishing infrastructure) that fronts a real site and captures post-login session cookies, demonstrating why legacy 2FA alone does not protect a session. Requires a domain you control, TLS, and dedicated infrastructure; the reference tool for authorized MFA-phishing exercises.
tools.when: When your authorized red-team scope includes proving session-token exposure or comparing legacy 2FA against phishing-resistant FIDO2/passkeys in your own environment.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/kgretzky/evilginx2 && cd evilginx2 && make

tools.name: Modlishka
tools.desc: Go reverse proxy that transparently proxies a whole multi-domain HTTPS site through a single phishing domain and captures credentials and session tokens (authorized red-team phishing infrastructure). Pioneered the modern Adversary-in-the-Middle technique in research; its author restricts use to authorized testing and defensive awareness.
tools.when: Authorized engagements that need whole-domain transparent proxying without client certificate installs, or historical demos of the AitM technique.

tools.name: CredSniper
tools.desc: Flask/Jinja2 framework serving cloned multi-step login pages (username → password → 2FA token) with Let's Encrypt SSL and an API for collected submissions. Unmaintained since 2020; use only in authorized test campaigns.
tools.when: Small scoped engagements that want a page-only credential collector with a results API; prefer Evilginx2/Modlishka for session-level testing.

tools.name: EvilGophish
tools.desc: Combines the Gophish campaign engine with an evilginx2-class reverse proxy in one toolchain so an authorized red team can schedule phishing emails and capture session tokens from a single console.
tools.when: When you want Evilginx2-grade token capture plus Gophish-style campaign scheduling and reporting in one deployment.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/fin3ss3g0d/EvilGophish && cd EvilGophish && sudo bash setup.sh

tools.name: zphisher
tools.desc: Automated login-page cloning kit with 30+ ready templates for email and social platforms, served over localhost, cloudflared, or ngrok links with submissions logged locally. The most widely used open tool for building credential-phishing awareness demos.
tools.when: Entry-level awareness demos or in-house training where a ready-made lookalike login page is enough and no campaign engine is needed.
tools.install: git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/htr-tech/zphisher && cd zphisher && bash zphisher.sh

tools.name: PhishX
tools.desc: Front-end-driven spear-phishing field kit (maintained fork of the original noobhackers PhishX) with ready login-page templates, tunnel serving, and a web dashboard for collected submissions and visit metadata. Authorized awareness use only.
tools.when: Fast, lightweight setup for cloning a social/email logon page and serving it from a tunnel during in-house training.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/rezaaksa/PhishX && cd PhishX && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Credential Harvester (SET)
tools.desc: SET's website-cloner + credential-harvester module: pulls a live login page, serves a lookalike, and logs POSTed usernames/passwords with a redirect after capture. Ships inside SET; use only against your own organization's employees in scoped campaigns.
tools.when: A single-page password-capture exercise without building a full framework — run it from the SET menu when authorized.

tools.name: PhishMailer
tools.desc: Generates realistic HTML and plain-text email messages with attachments for in-house phishing simulations, including per-recipient personalization and SMTP sending. Fills the content-creation step in authorized awareness campaigns.
tools.when: When you need convincing message and attachment content to feed into Gophish or your own SMTP as part of an approved simulation.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/BiZken/PhishMailer && cd PhishMailer && pip install -r requirements.txt

domains.name: Privilege Escalation (Linux & Windows)
domains.tagline: Local audit of Linux & Windows privilege boundaries: lax permissions, exposed SUID/sudo surface, scheduler jobs, and unpatched escalations — on systems you own.

tools.name: LinPEAS
tools.desc: Runs hundreds of privilege-boundary checks — SUID/GUID binaries, writable PATHs, cron entries, capabilities, credentials in files, known-vuln hints — on Linux/Unix/MacOS and color-codes findings by severity.
tools.when: First pass on any Linux host you are authorized to assess; `-s` for a faster/stealthier run, `-e` to enable extra checks before you dig into anything manually.

tools.name: LinEnum
tools.desc: Single-shell-script Linux enumeration collecting user, sudo, cron, SUID, PATH, and file-permission checks into one grep-able report; still ships as the Kali/BlackArch `linenum` package.
tools.when: A quick, dependency-free sweep when you want a portable .sh you can drop on a box and read results calmly offline.

tools.name: linux-smart-enumeration (lse)
tools.desc: Ranked Linux enumerator that reveals findings progressively by importance level (-l0..-l2) and can watch for recurring cron/process activity while it runs.
tools.when: When you want signal-first output instead of a full dump; escalate verbosity only if the default level comes up empty.

tools.name: linuxprivchecker
tools.desc: Python script that enumerates base system info and hunts world-writable files, misconfigurations, and cleartext passwords; written to suggest investigation targets rather than run exploits.
tools.when: An OSCP-friendly second opinion after LinPEAS when you want a leaner, Python-based cross-check on the same host.

tools.name: unix-privesc-check
tools.desc: PentestMonkey's classic shell script for weak file permissions and simple escalation vectors (world-writable files, exposed .netrc/.ssh), packaged in Kali; mature but only lightly maintained.
tools.when: A conservative, read-only check on aged Unix boxes (also Solaris/AIX/HP-UX) where you want a second, low-noise opinion on file-permission drift.
tools.install: sudo apt install unix-privesc-check && unix-privesc-check standard

tools.name: WinPEAS
tools.desc: Windows counterpart to LinPEAS from the same PEASS suite: scans services, scheduled tasks, unquoted paths, AlwaysInstallElevated, stored credentials, and patch gaps; ships as winPEAS.exe (x64/x86) and winPEAS.bat in one release.
tools.when: First pass on any Windows host you are authorized to assess; run as a low-integrity user, then re-run elevated to compare the privilege surface.

tools.name: Seatbelt
tools.desc: GhostPack C# host-survey tool bundling dozens of 'safety-check' modules (token privileges, services, autoruns, credential stores, scheduled tasks) runnable in grouped or single-command mode.
tools.when: Focused follow-up enumeration when you need a specific answer (e.g. only TokenPrivileges, Services, or the LOLBAS module); supports clean txt/json output.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/GhostPack/Seatbelt && cd Seatbelt && dotnet build -c Release

tools.name: Windows-Exploit-Suggester (legacy)
tools.desc: The 2014 original that coined the term; now archived because it depends on Microsoft's Security Bulletin Excel dump, which has been frozen since Q1 2017 — it can only address XP/Vista-era systems.
tools.when: Only retro lab images from before 2017; for any current Windows host use WES-NG, which reads the live MSRC feed instead.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/GDSSecurity/Windows-Exploit-Suggester && cd Windows-Exploit-Suggester && python windows-exploit-suggester.py --update

tools.name: linux-exploit-suggester
tools.desc: Off-host Linux audit tool (LES): reads kernel/distro fingerprints and cross-references them against current public exploit/PoC sets to rank exposure to known local privilege-escalation bugs.
tools.when: After enumeration, when you want a ranked, CVE-linked shortlist of which kernel-era exploits are plausibly worth testing on your own lab or CTF hosts.

tools.name: WES-NG (wesng)
tools.desc: Windows Exploit Suggester - Next Generation: takes a `systeminfo` dump (or missing-patch list) and maps it against a continuously updated MSRC/NVD dataset to list missing patches and known exploits.
tools.when: Grab `systeminfo` from your Windows lab host, run wes.py on your workstation, and correlate patches offline for any supported OS from XP to Windows 11.
tools.install: pip install wesng && wes.py --update && wes.py systeminfo.txt

tools.name: linux-exploit-suggester-2
tools.desc: Perl-based next-gen suggester that matches kernel/package versions against an exploit-db-derived list and can pull matching PoCs for review.
tools.when: A second candidate shortlist when LES disagrees, or old-style searching where you want the actual exploit source downloaded into your lab to read first.

tools.name: GTFOBins
tools.desc: Reference site (not a tool): documents how standard Unix binaries — when sudo, SUID, or capability-misconfigured — can escape restricted contexts, read/write files, or escalate.
tools.when: Look up every SUID binary and sudo rule your enumeration surfaced; if the binary is listed, the page shows the exact boundary you wrongly granted.

tools.name: LOLBAS
tools.desc: Windows sibling of GTFOBins: catalogs living-off-the-land binaries, scripts, and libraries that legitimate shipped Windows components can be coerced into doing beyond their intended job.
tools.when: Cross-check any signed binary or allowlisted script your enumeration surfaces on a Windows host — each entry lists the exact abuse command and MITRE mapping.

tools.name: Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847)
tools.desc: Root POC for CVE-2022-0847 (Linux 5.8–5.16.x): abuses an uninitialized pipe_buffer flag to overwrite read-only page-cache data; this build overwrites /etc/passwd and restores it after popping a shell.
tools.when: On lab or CTF kernels inside the affected range when no misconfiguration path exists; expect it to fail cleanly on 5.16.11+ or backported-fix kernels.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/Arinerron/CVE-2022-0847-DirtyPipe-Exploit && cd CVE-2022-0847-DirtyPipe-Exploit && gcc -o exploit exploit.c && ./exploit

tools.name: dirtycow (CVE-2016-5195)
tools.desc: The archived Dirty COW race-condition family (CVE-2016-5195) for kernels roughly up to 4.8.3: PoCs write into read-only mappings, e.g. splicing a new root account into /etc/passwd.
tools.when: Only legacy or sandboxed images that still run pre-2016-fix kernels; treat it as a historical exercise — modern distros are not exposed.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/firefart/dirtycow && cd dirtycow && gcc -pthread dirty.c -o dirty -lcrypt && ./dirty

tools.name: PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034)
tools.desc: Qualys-reported pkexec (polkit) memory-corruption exploit giving a one-command root shell on unpatched systems; technically a setuid userspace flaw, not the kernel, but near-unrivaled in reliability when present.
tools.when: Applies to many distros of 2009–2022 vintage; `make dry-run` tests whether your own host is vulnerable without popping a shell.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/berdav/CVE-2021-4034 && cd CVE-2021-4034 && make && ./cve-2021-4034

tools.name: pspy
tools.desc: Unprivileged process snooper: uses /proc scans triggered by inotify events to catch short-lived processes (cron jobs, root scripts, and the arguments they carry) that a normal `ps` sweep never sees.
tools.when: Park it for a couple of minutes after enumeration on a Linux host; timing-dependent scheduler jobs that static scans miss appear as they fire.

tools.name: inotifywait
tools.desc: inotify-based file/directory event watcher (create/modify/access/delete) from the inotify-tools package; the building block for precise, pattern-able watching scripts.
