tools.when: Point it at a specific writable directory or config file (e.g. a scheduler-owned path) and see exactly when and which files change on boxes you own.

tools.name: fatrace
tools.desc: fanotify-based system-wide file-access reporter (read/write/open/close per PID and path) — useful when a scheduled job touches files too briefly for process listing to catch.
tools.when: Wide-surface file watching on your own host where inotify recursion gets unwieldy; narrow it with `--dir` to a single directory of interest.
tools.install: sudo apt install fatrace && sudo fatrace --dir /var/spool

domains.name: Reconnaissance & OSINT
domains.tagline: Passive + active discovery: subdomains, DNS, historical data, people, leaks, and exposed assets.

tools.name: Amass
tools.desc: OWASP-recommended, querying dozens of sources for active/passive subdomains; builds graph and flagship-level relationships between discovered assets.
tools.when: Full-scope startup: let it run long against a big target while you work other recon.

tools.name: Subfinder
tools.desc: Fast passive-only subdomain discovery from 30+ sources (APIs optional, works well without them).
tools.when: The daily driver when you want speed over depth, or when API keys are scarce.

tools.name: crt.sh
tools.desc: Transparency-log search over issued TLS certificates; zero-install, browser or curl.
tools.when: Instant no-setup check; great for history not visible via simple DNS queries.

tools.name: dnsx
tools.desc: Fast multi-threaded DNS resolver built to verify a big list of candidate subdomains (A/AAAA/CNAME/TXT).
tools.when: After enumeration: confirm which hosts resolve and grab their records in one pass.

tools.name: httpx
tools.desc: Probes a list of hosts and returns live status codes, technologies, titles, and fingerprints.
tools.when: Convert hundreds of DNS names into a live-but-quiet target list before tooling takes over.

tools.name: SecurityTrails
tools.desc: Passive DNS history and subdomain API; free tier without keys.
tools.when: See records that no longer resolve but reveal old infrastructure (staging, dev).

tools.name: VirusTotal DNS
tools.desc: Relations/passive-dns endpoints to map infrastructure and finding subdomains via historical resolution.
tools.when: Correlate IP→domains and flag anomalies when you already have an API key.

tools.name: naabu
tools.desc: Fast SYN port scanner (projectdiscovery) focused on top 100/1000 ports; integrates cleanly with httpx/nuclei.
tools.when: Quick-but-broad port discovery feeding the rest of the pipeline.

tools.name: Masscan
tools.desc: Most-port-fastest scanner; emits results in a format easily piped into nmap or naabu.
tools.when: Scan the entire internet range of your target (or very large CIDRs) quickly.

tools.name: nmap
tools.desc: The classic suite: port scan, OS/service detection, and scripting engine (NSE).
tools.when: Deep service identification and vulnerability scripts on a small, targeted set of hosts.

tools.name: RustScan
tools.desc: Rust-based scanner that sweeps all ports in seconds then hands specifics to nmap.
tools.when: When you want all-ports coverage faster than nmap's default and the pipeline output into nmap.

domains.name: Red Team Infrastructure & Operations
domains.tagline: Authorized red team tooling: pivoting, tunnels, proxying, and practice lab environments.

tools.name: sshuttle
tools.desc: Lightweight VPN-like pivot using SSH; routes traffic through a jump host without requiring root on the target.
tools.when: Need simple, reliable lateral routing to access internal networks from a single jump host during authorized engagements or labs.

tools.name: chisel
tools.desc: Fast TCP/HTTP tunneling over a single port with reverse or forward modes; portable and minimal.
tools.when: Tunneling a specific service through restrictive firewalls or NAT during controlled testing.

tools.name: ligolo-ng
tools.desc: TUN-based tunneling agent for pivoting with automatic routes; simple interface for authorized red team operations.
tools.when: Need full network access through a pivot host with automatic routing in a lab or authorized engagement environment.

tools.name: frp
tools.desc: Fast reverse proxy for exposing local services through a remote server; stable and well-documented.
tools.when: Need controlled reverse proxying for lab infrastructure or authorized test setups behind NAT.

tools.name: proxychains-ng
tools.desc: Force any TCP application through a chain of proxies for controlled routing in authorized testing.
tools.when: Need to route existing tooling through a proxy chain during authorized red team exercises or lab scenarios.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/rofl0r/proxychains-ng && cd proxychains-ng && ./configure --prefix=/usr && make && sudo make install

tools.name: GOAD
tools.desc: Great Oxide Active Directory lab for realistic, authorized red team practice with vulnerable AD domains.
tools.when: Practicing authorized AD attack/defense techniques in an isolated, controlled lab environment.

tools.name: VECTR
tools.desc: Purple team tracking and assessment framework for mapping techniques to MITRE ATT&CK in controlled exercises.
tools.when: Running structured, authorized red/purple team exercises with measurable objectives and reporting.

domains.name: Vulnerability Scanning & Assessment
domains.tagline: Automated detection of known CVEs and misconfigurations at scale, plus manual triage.

tools.name: Nuclei
tools.desc: Template-driven scanner (projectdiscovery) running thousands of YAML checks against your web, network, and infrastructure targets to confirm known CVEs and misconfigurations.
tools.when: First-pass automated sweep across a whole asset list; fast and CI-friendly enough to run on every build.

tools.name: Nessus
tools.desc: Tenable's market-standard commercial scanner with credentialed and remote checks across OSes, services, and web; the free Essentials tier covers a small lab.
tools.when: Deep credentialed findings and compliance-style reports on the servers you operate.
tools.install: sudo dpkg -i Nessus-10.x-ubuntu.deb  (free Essentials .deb from tenable.com)

tools.name: OpenVAS (GVM)
tools.desc: Greenbone's open-source stack forked from the old Nessus; schedules scans of thousands of network vulnerability tests (NVTs) with a web dashboard.
tools.when: Self-hosted, ongoing internal-network scanning without commercial licensing.
tools.install: sudo apt install gvm && sudo gvm-setup

tools.name: Vuls
tools.desc: Agentless Go scanner that runs from one control host over SSH to inventory OS packages, middleware, and containers, then maps each server to applicable CVEs.
tools.when: Fleet-level Linux vulnerability tracking when installing agents on every box is not an option.

tools.name: Nikto
tools.desc: Perl web server scanner running 7,000+ checks for known files, outdated software, and misconfigurations on your own sites.
tools.when: Fast baseline sweep of a web server's exposed surface before deeper application testing.

tools.name: OWASP ZAP
tools.desc: Full-featured open-source web app scanner combining an intercepting proxy, spidering, and automated active and passive scanning behind a REST API.
tools.when: DAST runs against the apps you build, or as the intercepting proxy for manual test sessions.

tools.name: Arachni
tools.desc: Feature-rich Ruby web app scanner with modular platform checks, a REST API, and distributed scanning of your own applications.
tools.when: Headless or scripted scans that need to scale across many of your endpoints from one controller.
tools.install: Download and extract the arachni release archive from GitHub

tools.name: sqlmap
tools.desc: Long-standing automated SQL injection detector with database fingerprinting; validates whether a suspected injection point on your own app is genuinely exploitable.
tools.when: Confirming and triaging reported SQLi findings on applications you own and operate.

tools.name: Nettacker
tools.desc: OWASP automation framework that scans your networks in layers (ports, services, subdomains), correlates the results, then runs follow-up module checks.
tools.when: Automating broad network discovery plus vulnerability checks against your own infrastructure in one pass.

tools.name: Vulners
tools.desc: Aggregated vulnerability and exploit database offering a free API plus an Nmap script that matches your scanned services against millions of CVEs.
tools.when: Enriching plain nmap service banners of your hosts with live CVE matches at no cost.
tools.install: Copy vulners.nse into /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ (get it from vulners.com)

tools.name: OpenSCAP
tools.desc: NIST-certified scanner applying security-policy content (CIS, STIG) and OVAL CVE definitions to your Linux hosts for compliance and vulnerability posture.
tools.when: Auditing your servers against published baselines and tracking CVE coverage across them.

tools.name: WPScan
tools.desc: WordPress scanner that fingerprints core, theme, and plugin versions against the WPScan vulnerability database and does user and weak-password checks.
tools.when: Regularly auditing the WordPress sites you maintain for outdated plugins and known CVEs.

tools.name: CMSmap
tools.desc: Python tool that scans WordPress, Joomla, and Drupal sites you own for known vulnerabilities and exposed file paths.
tools.when: A single-command health check across mixed small-CMS estates without installing separate scanners.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/Dionach/CMSmap && cd CMSmap && python3 cmsmap.py

tools.name: droopescan
tools.desc: Lightweight Perl scanner focused on Drupal, with partial WordPress and Bolt coverage; strong on plugin and module fingerprinting.
tools.when: Targeted assessments of the Drupal sites in your fleet.

tools.name: Trivy
tools.desc: Aqua's scanner that fingerprints vulnerable packages and CVEs in the container images, filesystems, IaC templates, and SBOMs you run.
tools.when: Adding vuln gates to your image builds and scanning local containers for known CVEs before deployment.

tools.name: Grype
tools.desc: Anchore's fast scanner pairing with Syft to map dependency CVEs across the containers and filesystems you build and ship.
tools.when: Container and directory scans where you also want an SBOM generated in the same workflow.

tools.name: osv-scanner
tools.desc: Google's scanner that matches your project lockfiles and SBOMs against the open-source-focused OSV.dev vulnerability database.
tools.when: Quick CI check of dependency lockfiles in your own repos against a community-maintained vuln feed.

tools.name: cve-bin-tool
tools.desc: Scans binary files and their strings to identify which known-vulnerable library and product components your software bundles.
tools.when: Checking compiled products you distribute for embedded third-party components with published CVEs.

tools.name: searchsploit / Exploit-DB
tools.desc: Offline grep over the ~40,000-entry Exploit-DB archive bundled with Kali, showing exploit scripts, Metasploit modules, and build instructions for your own lab.
tools.when: Looking up local proof-of-concept code to reproduce and verify a CVE on systems you control.

tools.name: cve-search
tools.desc: Local MongoDB-backed engine that ingests NVD, CISA, and Exploit-DB feeds for fast bulk lookups across your whole inventory.
tools.when: Correlating a large asset list against CVE data offline when you cannot rely on external APIs.

tools.name: NVD (NIST)
tools.desc: Official NIST vulnerability feed and web UI; the reference source for CVE metadata, CPE mappings, and CVSS metrics.
tools.when: Confirming identifiers, severity scores, and affected product lists for a CVE under review.

domains.name: Web Application Security
domains.tagline: The full web assessment stack: intercepting proxies, discovery, injection testing, API tooling, and OWASP-class vulnerability testing — nested by technique.

tools.name: Burp Suite
tools.desc: The de-facto intercepting proxy for manual testing: intercept/edit requests, inspect responses, map the app, and extend via a large BApp marketplace.
tools.when: Every manual web engagement; the default scratchpad for inspecting and shaping requests to an app you are authorized to test.

tools.name: OWASP ZAP
tools.desc: Free and open-source OWASP proxy with automated scanning, fuzzing, and a REST API for CI-driven baseline scanning.
tools.when: When you need a fully open, scriptable proxy with automated scanning you can drive from a pipeline against a staging app you own.

tools.name: Caido
tools.desc: Lightweight, modern intercepting proxy with a clean UI and fast request replay, built as a slim alternative to the heavyweight suites.
tools.when: When you want a quick, single-file proxy for interception and replay without a large install footprint.
tools.install: brew tap caido/caido && brew install caido

tools.name: ffuf
tools.desc: Extremely fast web fuzzer written in Go for directories, files, parameters, vhosts, and more; supports filters, recursion, and matchers.
tools.when: Anytime you need fast brute-force discovery of paths or parameters against a target you are authorized to test.

tools.name: gobuster
tools.desc: Simple multi-purpose fuzzer for directories, DNS subdomains, and virtual hosts using wordlists.
tools.when: When you want a lightweight, easy-to-script brute forcer without a big learning curve.

tools.name: feroxbuster
tools.desc: Fast, recursive content discovery fuzzer built in Rust that automatically scans discovered directories.
tools.when: When you want recursion and auto-re-scanning of found directories out of the box.

tools.name: dirsearch
tools.desc: Mature Python path scanner with threading, proxy support, and extensive filter/ignored-status options.
tools.when: When a simple, cross-platform Python scanner with many wordlist and output options is all you need.

tools.name: wfuzz
tools.desc: Flexible Python fuzzer for web content and parameter brute-forcing with rich payload/encoding options.
tools.when: When you need fine-grained iteration over multiple payload positions and encoding filters.

tools.name: sqlmap
tools.desc: The reference automated SQLi tool: detects and exploits injection in GET/POST/headers, enumerates DBMSes, and dumps data on targets you are authorized to test.
tools.when: When a parameter looks injectable and you want thorough detection plus DB fingerprinting, safe limits, and batch modes.

tools.name: NoSQLMap
tools.desc: Automated pentesting tool for NoSQL databases (MongoDB, CouchDB) injection and misconfiguration.
tools.when: When the backend is NoSQL and you need injection-point discovery against an app you own or have scope for.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/codingo/NoSQLMap && pip3 install -r NoSQLMap/requirements.txt

tools.name: Commix
tools.desc: Automated OS command injection detection and exploitation with support for many injection techniques and filter bypasses.
tools.when: When you suspect command injection in a parameter or header and want an automated detector on authorized targets.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/commixproject/commix && cd commix && python3 commix.py -h

tools.name: tplmap
tools.desc: Detects and exploits server-side template injection across engines (Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker, etc.).
tools.when: When an app renders user input inside templates and you need to confirm SSTI on a scope-authorized target.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/epinna/tplmap && pip3 install -r tplmap/requirements.txt

tools.name: Dalfox
tools.desc: Fast, parameter-analysis XSS scanner written in Go with payload generation and Telegram/Discord notification support.
tools.when: When you want to automate XSS discovery against a list of endpoints on authorized targets and pipeline results.

tools.name: XSStrike
tools.desc: XSS detection suite with payload crafting, bruteforce, and WAF/filter-detection heuristics.
tools.when: When you need sophisticated payload crafting and WAF detection for manual XSS validation in your tests.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/s0md3v/XSStrike && pip3 install -r XSStrike/requirements.txt

tools.name: mitmproxy
tools.desc: Interactive man-in-the-middle proxy with a powerful scriptable (Python) add-on API for request shaping and inspection.
tools.when: When you need programmatic control over intercepted API traffic (rewrite, capture, fuzz) in your tests.

tools.name: Postman
tools.desc: API client and collection runner for crafting, saving, and automating HTTP requests against services under test.
tools.when: When you need organized collections, environments, and simple automation to reason about an API's behavior.

tools.name: HTTPie
tools.desc: User-friendly command-line HTTP client with readable, colorful output for quick manual requests.
tools.when: For fast ad-hoc requests in a terminal during investigation without a heavyweight GUI.

tools.name: jwt_tool
tools.desc: Audits JSON Web Tokens: signature verification, algorithm confusion, and known CVE checks against tokens issued by apps you test.
tools.when: When an application uses JWTs and you need to inspect claims, check alg:none/confusion, and validate signing secrets.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ticarpi/jwt_tool && cd jwt_tool && python3 jwt_tool.py -h

tools.name: smuggler
tools.desc: Detects HTTP request smuggling variants (CL.TE, TE.CL, TE.TE obfuscation) against backend parsing mismatches.
tools.when: When a stack splits differently between proxies/back-ends and you want to test smuggling scenarios on authorized targets.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/defparam/smuggler && python3 smuggler.py regex.txt urls.txt

domains.name: Wireless & Bluetooth Security
domains.tagline: WiFi capture and cracking, RF spectrum analysis, WPS auditing, and Bluetooth — for testing networks and gear you own or are authorized to audit.

tools.name: aircrack-ng
tools.desc: The reference 802.11 suite: captures WEP and WPA/WPA2-PSK handshakes, cracks them against wordlists/dictionaries, and verifies recovered keys; ships the airodump-ng and aireplay-ng binaries.
tools.when: Start every authorized Wi-Fi audit here: put a supported adapter into monitor mode and validate the key strength and fallback behavior of your own AP.

tools.name: airodump-ng
tools.desc: Packet-capture and display tool that enumerates nearby access points and clients, logs capture files, and grabs 4-way handshakes for offline cracking.
tools.when: Any authorized Wi-Fi audit needs it first: channel-by-channel capture of BSSIDs, signal, encryption type, and handshake material on hardware you run.

tools.name: aireplay-ng
tools.desc: Frame-injection and replay tool of the suite: sends deauthentication frames and replays captured packets to trigger a fresh 4-way handshake when a station won't associate on its own.
tools.when: On a lab client that sits idle, use deauth to force a new handshake so you can verify your own PSK policy faster.

tools.name: Wifite2
tools.desc: Automated Wi-Fi auditing wrapper: scans with a monitor-mode adapter, lets you pick targets from a menu, and chains deauth, handshake capture, and cracking (or WPS PIN work via bully/reaver) in one run.
tools.when: Fast repeatable lab checks on your own networks where you want the whole capture-to-crack pipeline driven from a single interactive menu.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/derv82/wifite2.git && cd wifite2 && sudo python3 setup.py install

tools.name: hcxdumptool
tools.desc: Raw PCAPNG capture tool for PMKID and handshake material using a single adapter; often the fastest way to gather WPA test data without injection tricks.
tools.when: Verify PSK strength on an AP you own that advertises PMKID — one passive-ish run beats orchestrating deauths.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ZerBea/hcxdumptool.git && cd hcxdumptool && make && sudo make install

tools.name: Kismet
tools.desc: Multi-protocol passive wireless detector and logging framework; captures and tracks 802.11, Bluetooth, and SDR sources with server + web UI.
tools.when: Long-running passive surveys and signal mapping of your own test environment, plus intrusion detection on your authorized airspace.

tools.name: Wireshark
tools.desc: Universal packet dissector with deep 802.11 and Bluetooth protocol support; decrypts WPA/EAPOL traffic when supplied the PMK/keys.
tools.when: Post-capture forensics: walk frame-by-frame through handshakes, probe requests, and BT packets from your own gear to understand protocol behavior.

tools.name: gqrx
tools.desc: Software-defined radio receiver built on GNU Radio; tunes an RTL-SDR dongle and demodulates, decodes, and spectrally displays received signals.
tools.when: Scan the ISM band around your lab to identify transmitters or interference sources before blaming your own Wi-Fi gear.

tools.name: RTL-SDR
tools.desc: Cheap USB software-defined radio receiver with drivers and command-line utilities (rtl_fm, rtl_tcp, rtl_test) for raw spectral sampling.
tools.when: The base RF monitoring hardware and tooling: stream IQ captures into gqrx or inspectrum for analysis of signals in your own environment.

tools.name: inspectrum
tools.desc: Offline signal-analysis tool that renders recorded IQ or audio files into an interactive waterfall for visual protocol and modulation identification.
tools.when: Analyze captured RF bursts (from RTL-SDR or other taps) to spot modulation patterns and packet structures after the fact.

tools.name: horst
tools.desc: Lightweight ncurses 802.11 traffic analyzer with channel scanning, signal histograms, and per-client statistics in a terminal.
tools.when: A minimal TUI alternative to Kismet for quick signal and traffic checks in the field on authorized networks.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/br101/horst && cd horst && make && sudo make install

tools.name: Ubertooth
tools.desc: Open-source 2.4 GHz radio hardware plus host software for Bluetooth capture and injection; analyzes frequency-hopping patterns, Classic BT, and BLE advertising on the Ubertooth One dongle.
tools.when: Hardware-level Bluetooth auditing of your own peripherals: sniffing hop patterns, identifying weak pairing, and verifying advertising behavior.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/greatscottgadgets/ubertooth && cd ubertooth/host && mkdir build && cd build && cmake .. && make && sudo make install

tools.name: bettercap
tools.desc: Modular network attack/monitoring framework whose Bluetooth modules enumerate and intercept BLE and Classic BT devices and connections from the local host.
tools.when: Scriptable Bluetooth enumeration and connection monitoring against your own test devices without extra RF hardware.

tools.name: btlejack
tools.desc: Sniffs and interacts with BLE advertising and connection channels using nRF24-family USB dongles; supports jamming and session recovery using previously captured keys.
tools.when: Low-cost BLE protocol auditing of your own accessories: map advertising channels and check whether session keys are reused across connections.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/virtualabs/btlejack && cd btlejack && make && sudo make install

tools.name: BlueZ
tools.desc: The Linux Bluetooth protocol stack: hcitool, hcidump, btmon, and bluetoothctl expose controller state, HCI packets, and link logs.
tools.when: Free, instant BT visibility on Linux before reaching for dedicated hardware like Ubertooth.

tools.name: Reaver
tools.desc: The reference WPS PIN brute-force tool: probes the registrar PIN transaction logic and, on vulnerable APs in your lab, recovers the WPS PIN and derived WPA-PSK.
tools.when: Validate whether a lab AP's WPS implementation is brute-force resistant — many modern routers lock out after failures, which is the outcome you want to confirm.

tools.name: Wash
tools.desc: Companion scanner shipped with reaver that detects WPS-enabled access points and reads their WPS state (version, locked or not) without launching an active attack.
tools.when: Passive WPS recon across your own network estate before deciding whether a PIN-based audit is even relevant.

tools.name: Bully
tools.desc: Reimplementation of the WPS PIN brute-force client in C with tighter packet timing and tolerance for flaky associations than reaver's original implementation.
tools.when: When reaver stalls against your own AP, Bully's more robust locking logic often completes the audit where reaver cannot.

domains.name: Application Security (SAST, DAST, Secrets & SCA)
domains.tagline: Product-security gates for the code and recipes you ship: SAST, DAST, secrets detection, dependency (SCA), and IaC scanning for dev and DevProd teams.

tools.name: Semgrep
tools.desc: Lightweight app-sec static analyzer for 30+ languages: YAML rules that read like the code they match, bundled security packs (p/security-audit, p/owasp-top-ten), and pre-commit/CI/IDE hooks; the free CLI covers single-function/file patterns while the commercial AppSec Platform adds cross-function taint.
tools.when: The default SAST layer for any dev team: run it per-PR in CI or in the editor to catch injection, dangerous-API misuse, and hardcoded secrets before merge.

tools.name: SonarQube
tools.desc: Self-hosted code-quality and security platform: the free LGPL Community Edition runs hundreds of static rules over 30+ languages with dashboards, quality gates, and trended security reports; paid tiers add branch analysis and deeper coverage.
tools.when: When an org needs a shared, dashboard-visible quality gate and SAST history instead of per-commit CLI output.

tools.name: CodeQL
tools.desc: GitHub's query-based analysis engine that databases your code and runs QL queries to find vulnerability classes; the CLI is free, and the strongest maintained rule sets ship through GitHub code scanning.
tools.when: High-signal coverage on GitHub-hosted repos: enable code scanning on schedules and PRs, then drop into the CodeQL CLI to run or author bespoke queries on a local database.
tools.install: Download the CodeQL CLI bundle from github.com/github/codeql-action/releases

tools.name: Bandit
tools.desc: PyCQA's AST-based Python analyzer that flags common first-party security mistakes - SQLi, shell injection, pickles, eval, weak crypto, and path permissions - with a low-noise report of findings you can tune.
tools.when: A no-config SAST pass for Python services: pip-install, point it at the package directory, and wire into CI.

tools.name: gosec
tools.desc: SecureGo's Go static analyzer walking ASTs and data flow to find hardcoded creds, weak TLS configs, unsafe sql/exec sinks, and integer-overflow risk in first-party Go code.
tools.when: The quick Go-specific SAST gate in CI, alongside or before a language-agnostic scanner like Semgrep.

tools.name: OWASP ZAP
tools.desc: Full web/API security scanner: intercepting proxy, spider, passive + active scanning, and a programmable REST API; ships zap-baseline.py and Docker images ready for automated CI DAST against the apps you deploy.
tools.when: Stand up per-app DAST: run the baseline scan against a staging build nightly or per-PR, then use the proxy for manual testing of tricky auth and authorization flows.

tools.name: Burp Suite Community
tools.desc: PortSwigger's leading web application testing platform: the free Community Edition gives you the intercepting proxy, a searchable request/response history, and Repeater/Decoder/Comparer manual tools; the automated scanner requires paid Pro or Enterprise editions.
tools.when: Manual pentest-style review of your own apps: drive the app through the proxy, then replay, tamper, and fuzz individual requests by hand.
tools.install: preinstalled (web) - free Community download from portswigger.net

tools.name: RESTler
tools.desc: Microsoft's stateful REST API fuzzer: ingests your OpenAPI spec, infers producer-consumer request dependencies, then fuzzes request sequences against the live service to surface 5xx crashes, resource leaks, and security-checker violations.
tools.when: API-only DAST beyond the HTML UI: after a ZAP baseline, point RESTler at the schema to grind through every endpoint and parameter combination.
tools.install: Download the RESTler release archive from github.com/microsoft/restler-fuzzer/releases

tools.name: Gitleaks
tools.desc: Fastest OSS secret scanner: a single Go binary that sweeps full git history or plain directories with 200+ regex rules for API keys, tokens, and passwords, exporting JSON/SARIF, with pre-commit and GitHub Action hooks.
tools.when: Gate every repo and pipeline: full-history sweep when onboarding, then pre-commit/PR scans from then on; the default before anything heavier.

tools.name: TruffleHog
tools.desc: Secret scanner (trufflesecurity) with 600+ credential detectors that actively verify matches against vendor APIs to separate live credentials from noise; scans git, GitHub/GitLab orgs, S3, Docker, and filesystems.
tools.when: Org-wide and history-hardening sweeps where knowing which leaked credentials still work matters more than raw match counts.

tools.name: detect-secrets
tools.desc: Yelp's Python scanner that audits a repo once into a .secrets.baseline then diffs only new lines in pre-commit/CI, so only genuinely new secrets get flagged instead of the same approved ones on every run.
tools.when: Teams worn out by re-flagged false positives: do the one-time audit + baseline review, then let it police new commits.

tools.name: git-secrets
tools.desc: AWS Labs' original git-hook guard that registers grep patterns (including a ready AWS credential set) as client-side commit hooks so secrets never land in history; legacy and effectively unmaintained.
tools.when: Last-resort hook-only protection on old, isolated repos - otherwise reach for Gitleaks or TruffleHog.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/awslabs/git-secrets && cd git-secrets && make install

tools.name: OWASP Dependency-Check
tools.desc: OWASP's SCA utility that fingerprints declared dependencies (Java, .NET, Python, Node, Ruby, Go, Rust, and more) against NVD and other feeds, emitting HTML/XML reports of CVSS-scored known-CVE matches; ships CLI, Gradle/Maven plugins, and a GitHub Action.
tools.when: The reference dependency gate for build output: run on release builds to block known-vulnerable libraries before they ship; the first run downloads the full NVD feed, so schedule it early.

tools.name: osv-scanner
tools.desc: Google's open-source vulnerability scanner (the engine behind GitHub Dependabot) that matches your lockfiles and SBOMs against the OSV.dev database - fast, quiet, and free of NVD feed friction.
tools.when: Snappy per-lockfile check in CI (package-lock.json, go.sum, requirements, poetry, etc.) when you want OSV-only coverage without a heavyweight feed.

tools.name: pip-audit
tools.desc: Python Packaging Authority's scanner that audits direct and transitive PyPI requirements against OSV/advisory feeds, and can even auto-fix vulnerable packages installed locally (--fix).
tools.when: Python-only repos: the smallest honest way to keep requirements.txt/pyproject dependency lists clean as part of pre-commit or CI.

tools.name: Checkov
tools.desc: Prisma Cloud-maintained IaC static analyzer with 1,000+ built-in policies for Terraform (incl. plan output), CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Helm, Dockerfile, Bicep, ARM, and Serverless; graph-based and multi-resource aware, with Python/YAML custom policies.
tools.when: The default IaC gate: scan Terraform/K8s/Dockerfile in CI and on terraform plan to catch exposed resources, weak IAM, and missing encryption before apply.

tools.name: KICS
tools.desc: Checkmarx's open-source IaC scanner (Keeping Infrastructure as Code Secure) running thousands of queries across 20+ platforms - Terraform, Kubernetes, Docker, Helm, CloudFormation, Ansible - with SARIF/SonarQube output and custom queries via OPA/Rego.
tools.when: A complementary cross-check on IaC after Checkov, or the pick when you want OPA/Rego policy authoring (the slot that archived Terrascan used to fill).

domains.name: Blue Team — Defense & Detection
domains.tagline: Tools defenders run to detect, monitor, and protect their own estate: SIEM, endpoint telemetry, network monitoring, and hostile-HTTP defense.

tools.name: Elastic Stack (ELK)
tools.desc: Reference open-core SIEM: ingests logs via Beats/Elastic Agent into Elasticsearch (Kibana for UI), and runs the detection engine with EQL/ES|QL/Sigma rules, dashboards, and built-in threat hunting.
tools.when: Your first-stop SIEM when you want one cluster for security detections plus powerful full-text log search and can absorb Elasticsearch operations.
tools.install: docker run -d -p 9200:9200 -e discovery.type=single-node docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:9.5.1 (then add Kibana + Elastic Agent per the docs)

tools.name: Wazuh
tools.desc: Open-source XDR/SIEM pairing an Elastic/OpenSearch backend with a unified agent delivering file-integrity monitoring, security configuration assessment, vulnerability detection, active response, and compliance dashboards.
tools.when: When you want SIEM plus endpoint agent in one cohesive open bundle with built-in compliance reporting (PCI-DSS/HIPAA/SOC 2) and less manual Elasticsearch plumbing.

tools.name: Splunk
tools.desc: Commercial SIEM incumbent (Cisco-owned): SPL search over indexed events, mature dashboards/alerts, and the largest third-party integration ecosystem; licensed per GB/day.
tools.when: When budget exists and you need enterprise SIEM tooling, best-in-class search UX, and vendor support — or as the benchmark when evaluating an all-open stack.

tools.name: Graylog
tools.desc: Open-source log management and SIEM on Elasticsearch/OpenSearch storage, with flexible extraction pipelines (streams + pipeline rules) for parsing, routing, GEOIP, and threat-intel enrichment.
tools.when: Log centralization when you want clean server-side pipelines to poll, enrich, and route messages into destinations like Splunk or Elastic — without running agent fleets or Wazuh-style XDR.
tools.install: curl -L -o graylog-repo.deb https://packages.graylog2.org/repo/packages/graylog-7.1-repository_latest.deb && sudo dpkg -i graylog-repo.deb && sudo apt-get install graylog-server

tools.name: Logstash
tools.desc: Data-shaping pipeline (the 'L' in ELK) that pulls logs and metrics, transforms them — parse, enrich, filter, route — and ships them to Elasticsearch or any other output.
tools.when: The standalone parsing/enrichment middle layer when an agent's native handling or a Beats module isn't enough for messy or appliance-shaped log sources.

tools.name: Velociraptor
tools.desc: Open-source DFIR + endpoint-monitoring framework (Rapid7): the Velociraptor Query Language hunts the entire fleet for forensic artifacts, collects live evidence at scale, and the monitoring engine runs Sigma detections against ETW/eBPF events in real time.
tools.when: Endpoint hunting and incident response at scale — triage thousands of hosts, collect volatile evidence, then keep them monitored with live detections.

tools.name: osquery
tools.desc: SQL-powered agent that exposes OS state — processes, sockets, files, users, listeners — as queryable tables; defenders fire fleet-wide queries instantly and schedule packs for continuous inspection, managed via Fleet.
tools.when: Lightweight cross-platform endpoint telemetry when you want to 'SELECT' answers from every host and ship the results to a SIEM; pair with Fleet (fleetdm) for enroll/query management.

tools.name: Sysmon
tools.desc: Windows Sysinternals driver that logs high-fidelity process creation, network connections, and file writes beyond default auditing; pair with the SwiftOnSecurity (or Modular) config for a solid threat-hunting baseline.
tools.when: On every Windows host where you need attacker-action visibility and can ship its event log to your SIEM — no heavy agent required.

tools.name: LimaCharlie
tools.desc: Cloud-native SecOps platform: an EDR sensor streams verbose endpoint telemetry over TLS in real time, and a YAML-based Detection & Response engine runs the full open Sigma ruleset with automated response actions.
tools.when: When you want EDR plus detection-as-code in the cloud without running a SIEM or agent server yourself; the free Community org covers small estates and labs.
tools.install: preinstalled (SaaS) — create a free Community org at limacharlie.io, then run the per-OS sensor installer and enable the Sigma ruleset

tools.name: Suricata
tools.desc: OISF's multi-threaded open-source IDS/IPS engine that inspects traffic with Snort-compatible rules at multi-Gbps speeds and emits structured EVE JSON alerts (plus PCAP) straight into your SIEM.
tools.when: High-throughput signature detection at your network edge or segmentation points; the default pick for a self-managed NIDS with IPS fallback.
tools.install: sudo add-apt-repository ppa:oisf/suricata-stable && sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install suricata && sudo suricata-update

tools.name: Snort 3
tools.desc: Cisco's next-generation open-source NIDS/IPS: Snort 3 adds multi-threading, a Lua-based policy language, and faster pattern matching over the classic 2.x line, tuned via Talos rules.
tools.when: When you prefer Cisco's Talos rules ecosystem, are migrating an existing Snort 2 deployment, or want SnortML-driven engine tuning.
tools.install: sudo apt-get install snort3 (Ubuntu 22.04+; otherwise build from the source tarball on snort.org)

tools.name: Zeek
tools.desc: Passive network-analysis framework (formerly Bro) that logs rich protocol metadata, file hashes, and events across 70+ log types for later forensics instead of blocking in real time.
tools.when: Deep protocol visibility feeding a SIEM or full-packet archive — run it beside Suricata/Snort because it answers 'what happened', while the engine answers 'alert'.
tools.install: docker pull zeek/zeek (or add the zeek.org apt repo: sudo apt-get install zeek)

tools.name: Security Onion
tools.desc: Turnkey NSM distribution that bundles Suricata (detection + full packet capture), Zeek metadata, Elasticsearch/Kibana dashboards, osquery host visibility, and alert/case management into a single install.
tools.when: Fastest way to stand up a complete detection-and-response platform on one box or a small grid when you don't want to assemble the components yourself.
tools.install: Download the ISO from https://securityonion.com, install, then run: sudo so-setup-network (guided wizard)

tools.name: ModSecurity
tools.desc: The OWASP open-source WAF engine (an OWASP Production project) that inspects HTTP traffic and enforces SecRule policies on Apache/nginx; load the OWASP CRS on top for real attack coverage.
tools.when: Inline HTTP-layer defense when you want the battle-tested rule ecosystem and can commit to tuning false positives against your apps.
tools.install: sudo apt-get install libapache2-mod-security2 (Apache; for nginx compile the module with --with-compat --add-dynamic-module=../ModSecurity-nginx)

tools.name: Coraza
tools.desc: OWASP WAF written in Go with near-full ModSecurity compatibility — runs CRS v4 without the legacy C engine as a library or middleware for Caddy, Traefik, APISIX, and API gateways, ideal for detection-as-code.
tools.when: Cloud-native stacks (Go services, containers, Caddy/Traefik/APISIX) where ModSecurity's build model is awkward but you still want CRS protection.
tools.install: xcaddy build --with github.com/corazawaf/coraza-caddy/v2 (then add the coraza_waf block to the Caddyfile)

tools.name: OWASP CRS
tools.desc: The OWASP flagship Core Rule Set — a community-maintained rule layer detecting SQLi, XSS, scanners, and other OWASP Top 10 attacks that runs on both ModSecurity and Coraza engines; a ruleset, not a standalone tool.
tools.when: The rule layer to load onto any WAF engine so a bare install actually detects web attacks; tune via the anomaly-scoring exclusions to cut false positives.
tools.install: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/coreruleset/coreruleset.git (then Include the CRS config in your WAF engine)

tools.name: Cloudflare WAF
tools.desc: Commercial managed edge WAF (SaaS) that filters traffic on Cloudflare's CDN using managed rulesets (including OWASP CRS coverage) plus bot and rate controls — no servers to run.
tools.when: When your apps already sit behind Cloudflare and you want managed rules, DDoS/bot defense, and zero self-hosting in one panel.
tools.install: preinstalled (SaaS) — enable in the dash.cloudflare.com Security panel, pick a managed ruleset, and tune via custom rules

domains.name: Cloud Security — AWS, Azure & GCP
domains.tagline: Posture, offense, and public-bucket checks across AWS, Azure, and GCP — for auditing your own accounts and sanctioned assessments.

tools.name: Prowler
tools.desc: Runs 1,000+ read-only checks across AWS, Azure, and GCP against CIS Benchmarks and 70+ compliance frameworks, with remediation guidance per finding.
tools.when: Kick off the posture review of any account you own; it is the default for CIS/NIST alignment across all three clouds and exposes findings via CLI or API.

tools.name: Scout Suite
tools.desc: NCC Group's multi-cloud auditor pulls configuration from provider APIs and renders a browsable point-in-time HTML report of risk areas for AWS, Azure, and GCP.
tools.when: When you want a clean visual report of config risk in one account as a second opinion alongside Prowler; last major release was 2022.

tools.name: CloudSploit
tools.desc: Aqua-maintained Node.js CSPM scanner for AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI, and GitHub misconfigurations with CIS/PCI/HIPAA compliance modes; also sold as the hosted Aqua Wave SaaS.
tools.when: Use the self-hosted scanner for broad multi-cloud config checks in CI; know that the actively maintained commercial route is the hosted Aqua Wave platform.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/aquasecurity/cloudsploit.git && cd cloudsploit && npm install

tools.name: S3Scanner
tools.desc: Scans lists of bucket names across AWS and S3-compatible stores (GCP, DigitalOcean, Linode, Scaleway) for existence, tests every permission path for misconfigurations, and can enumerate or dump objects.
tools.when: Find your own exposed buckets at scale: feed candidate names, get back which are public, listable, or readable.

tools.name: GCPBucketBrute
tools.desc: Enumerates Google Storage buckets from keyword permutations and reports per-bucket access, flagging public, writable, and privilege-escalation-prone buckets (storage.buckets.setIamPolicy).
tools.when: Check which of your GCS buckets are reachable or writable without auth, including permission escalations visible from a service account.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/RhinoSecurityLabs/GCPBucketBrute.git && cd GCPBucketBrute && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Pacu
tools.desc: The AWS exploitation framework: modular post-compromise attacks covering IAM privilege escalation, Lambda backdoors, log tampering, and EC2 RCE, with a session database for clean reporting.
tools.when: After you hold valid-but-least-privilege AWS keys and want to demonstrate what an attacker could escalate to; the offensive complement to Prowler on your own account.

tools.name: CloudFox
tools.desc: Bishop Fox's situational-awareness enumerator maps exploitable attack paths across AWS (34 commands) plus early Azure/GCP coverage, writing loot files for other tools.
tools.when: Run `cloudfox aws --profile X all-checks` first on any fresh AWS scope to learn the estate and spot privesc paths before deeper exploitation with Pacu.

tools.name: enumerate-iam
tools.desc: Brute-forces every read-only AWS API call against a credential set to print exactly which IAM permissions it holds.
tools.when: You recovered AWS keys of unknown privilege and need the permission list fast, before choosing an escalation path.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/andresriancho/enumerate-iam.git && cd enumerate-iam && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: IAMActionHunter
tools.desc: Collects and queries AWS IAM policy statements to surface users and roles holding privesc-relevant permissions (iam:create*, iam:put*...) and exports CSV; also ships as a Pacu module.
tools.when: Hunt least-privilege violations and privilege-escalation levers across a large account in minutes, then review the CSV.

tools.name: MicroBurst
tools.desc: NetSPI's PowerShell toolkit for attacking Azure: service discovery, weak-config auditing, credential dumping (AzPasswords), and post-exploitation on VMs, Key Vault, and Automation accounts.
tools.when: The default Azure toolkit in authenticated engagements; Windows-only, so run it from a PowerShell host with the Az modules installed.

tools.name: Stormspotter
tools.desc: Microsoft Azure Red Team's attack-graph tool: collects subscription and ARM resources into Neo4j and renders the attack surface with pivot opportunities.
tools.when: Map a large tenant visually and find cross-resource pivot paths once you hold reader-level access.

tools.name: ATEAM
tools.desc: NetSPI's unaudited reconnaissance tool probes name permutations across App Services, Key Vault, Storage, DevOps, SharePoint, and Databricks to discover Azure resources and attribute their tenant IDs.
tools.when: From outside, discover forgotten Azure resources whose names leak a tenant — ideal for attack-surface checks on your own domains before logging in.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/NetSPI/ATEAM.git && cd ATEAM && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: gcp-scanner
tools.desc: Google's scanner determines what a compromised credential can reach across GCE, GCS, GKE, Cloud SQL, BigQuery, KMS, and more, pulling from VM metadata, SA keys, or OAuth tokens.
tools.when: Assess blast radius after a leaked service account key or compromised VM, without needing gcloud installed.

tools.name: GCP IAM Privilege Escalation
tools.desc: Rhino's documented GCP IAM privesc methods plus a scanner (enumerate_member_permissions.py then check_for_privesc.py) that flags principals able to escalate.
tools.when: Audit who in your projects could privilege-escalate to org ownership and validate hardened role design.

tools.name: gcpwn
tools.desc: NetSPI's GCP and Workspace pentesting framework: enumerates and downloads project data, builds BloodHound OpenGraph models, and bundles credential and exploit tooling.
tools.when: Deep GCP/Workspace engagements where you want structured enumeration feeding BloodHound-style attack-path analysis.

domains.name: Container & Kubernetes Security
domains.tagline: Defending your own clusters: image scanning, SBOM, runtime detection, CIS posture, and admission policy.

tools.name: Trivy
tools.desc: Aqua Security's comprehensive scanner covering container images, filesystems, git repos, VMs, and Kubernetes; detects CVEs, misconfigurations, secrets, and licenses from one binary.
tools.when: Gate every image build in CI and scan at push time; add trivy-operator (or Kubescape) for in-cluster image monitoring.

tools.name: Grype
tools.desc: Anchore's fast vulnerability scanner for images, filesystems, and SBOMs; pairs with Syft and adds EPSS, KEV, and OpenVEX filtering to prioritize real risk.
tools.when: Speed-first CI scans, or scan an SBOM you already generated instead of re-pulling and re-analyzing the image.

tools.name: Syft
tools.desc: Generates SBOMs for container images, filesystems, and archives in CycloneDX, SPDX, and Syft JSON; feeds Grype directly and supports signed in-toto attestations.
tools.when: Produce a machine-readable dependency inventory at build time and ship it with the image to prove supply-chain provenance.

tools.name: Trivy
tools.desc: Cross-reference entry: `trivy image --format cyclonedx|spdx` emits SBOMs, and Trivy will also scan an existing SBOM document for vulnerabilities.
tools.when: You standardize on Trivy already and want SBOM output without introducing a second cataloging tool.

tools.name: cyclonedx-cli
tools.desc: OWASP CycloneDX CLI to validate, merge, diff, convert, sign, and verify CycloneDX and SPDX BOMs; exits non-zero on invalid input for CI gating.
tools.when: Normalize third-party vendor SBOMs into one format, diff releases to catch dependency drift, or enforce schema-valid BOMs in the pipeline.

tools.name: Falco
tools.desc: CNCF-graduated kernel monitoring agent (eBPF or driver) that watches syscalls enriched with container and Kubernetes metadata, alerting via a flexible rules engine.
tools.when: Deploy on every production node for real-time detection of shells in containers, privileged pods, and sensitive-file access.
tools.install: helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts && helm install falco falcosecurity/falco

tools.name: docker-bench-security
tools.desc: Docker's CIS Docker Benchmark script auditing the Docker/containerd host, daemon, and running containers against dozens of best-practice checks.
tools.when: Harden and periodically re-audit the container host after workloads are deployed; quick compliance readout for a single host.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/docker/docker-bench-security.git && cd docker-bench-security && sudo sh docker-bench-security.sh

tools.name: Kubescape
tools.desc: CNCF-incubating Kubernetes security platform scanning clusters, manifests, Helm charts, git repos, and images against CIS, NSA-CISA, and MITRE ATT&CK; operator mode adds continuous posture and eBPF runtime.
tools.when: First full-posture sweep of a cluster and as a CI gate on manifests; install the operator for continuous compliance monitoring.

tools.name: kube-bench
tools.desc: Aqua's Go tool that runs the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark against control plane, etcd, and worker node configuration, matched to the running Kubernetes version.
tools.when: Validate a specific hardened baseline after cluster upgrades, node onboarding, or as a scheduled per-node job.

tools.name: Popeye
tools.desc: Read-only live-cluster sanitizer that lints deployed workloads for misconfigurations, dead resources, port mismatches, and missing probes, scoring overall cluster health.
tools.when: Periodic 'wide-open' sweep to catch drift and operational debt that static manifest review misses.

tools.name: kube-hunter
tools.desc: Legacy Aqua pen-test tool that finds cluster weaknesses from an attacker's perspective (exposed dashboards, leaked secrets, weak RBAC); officially no longer under active development.
tools.when: Offense-style spot check on a cluster you own; treat findings as a starting list since it is not actively maintained.

tools.name: OPA Gatekeeper
tools.desc: CNCF policy controller that enforces Rego-based policy through constraint templates and constraints, with admission webhooks, audit, and mutation support.
tools.when: Enforce registry allowlists, required labels, and security-context rules at admission when you already know Rego or want the largest policy ecosystem.

tools.name: Kyverno
tools.desc: CNCF-graduated Kubernetes-native policy engine using YAML (no new language) to validate, mutate, generate, and clean up resources; verifies image signatures via cosign.
tools.when: Teams that prefer familiar YAML and want mutation, image verification, and policy-as-a-resource without learning Rego.
tools.install: helm repo add kyverno https://kyverno.github.io/helm-charts && helm install kyverno kyverno/kyverno -n kyverno --create-namespace

tools.name: Polaris
tools.desc: Fairwinds policy-as-code with 30+ built-in checks across security, networking, reliability, and efficiency; runs as a dashboard, CI CLI, or mutating admission webhook.
tools.when: Drop-in baseline enforcement with a visible compliance dashboard when full OPA or Kyverno is overkill.

tools.name: hadolint
tools.desc: Haskell Dockerfile linter that parses the Dockerfile AST and applies best-practice rules, delegating inline shell checks to ShellCheck (DL- and SC-prefixed findings).
tools.when: Lint Dockerfiles in CI to catch untagged images, root users, and unsafe RUN commands before the image is ever built.

tools.name: dockle
tools.desc: Container image linter that audits the built image against CIS Docker image checkpoints and best practices (non-root user, HEALTHCHECK, setuid/setgid files, content trust).
tools.when: Audit the built image itself, complementing Dockerfile lint, right before pushing to a production registry.

domains.name: Digital Forensics & Incident Response
domains.tagline: Analyze memory, disk, carved files, artifacts, and timelines from your own systems, lab evidence, and incident-response cases you legally possess.

tools.name: Volatility 3
tools.desc: The de-facto memory forensics framework: plugin-based analysis of RAM dumps (raw, EWF, crash/hibernation) across Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android — process listing, network artifacts, injected code, and more.
tools.when: Start here with any memory dump from a lab box or captured incident host; run pslist/pscan, netscan, and malfind to build the runtime picture.

tools.name: Volatility 2
tools.desc: The classic Python 2 framework (archived but stable) with the deepest plugin ecosystem and profile-based analysis for older Windows, Linux, and macOS dumps.
tools.when: Reach for it when a legacy or niche image lacks a Volatility 3 symbol table, or a plugin you need only exists in the classic tree.

tools.name: MemProcFS
tools.desc: Mounts a memory dump or live target (PCILeech FPGA/LeechAgent) as a virtual filesystem of processes, registry, and artifacts, with a batch forensic mode and YARA scanning.
tools.when: Fast interactive triage of a Windows dump without plugin CLI gymnastics, or live acquisition during your own incident response.

tools.name: Autopsy
tools.desc: GUI platform built on The Sleuth Kit: opens images and live drives, recovers deleted files, and runs ingest modules for web history, keyword search, and carving inside a case workflow.
tools.when: First-pass interactive examination of a drive or memory-card image from your own casework or a lab exercise — ingest everything, then drill into findings.

tools.name: The Sleuth Kit
tools.desc: Command-line suite for raw/EWF images: mmls for partition layout, fls/icat to list and extract inodes, istat for metadata, and tsk_recover for file recovery — the engine under Autopsy.
tools.when: Scripted or headless analysis, or when you need precise inode-level answers Autopsy hides behind its GUI.

tools.name: dc3dd
tools.desc: Forensic fork of GNU dd adding on-the-fly hashing, split output, pattern wiping, and detailed logging — evidence-grade imaging of a source drive to a file.
tools.when: Capture a definitive image of your own drive or USB stick before analysis so you examine the copy, not the live evidence.

tools.name: Guymager
tools.desc: GUI forensic imager for Linux producing flat (dd), EWF (E01), and AFF images with multi-threaded, pipelined reads for fast verified acquisitions.
tools.when: Click-driven imaging with progress bars and check-verification when you prefer a window over dc3dd's command line.

tools.name: foremost
tools.desc: Header/footer and data-structure file carver (originally from AFOSI) that extracts JPEG, ZIP, PDF, and other signatures from raw images or drives via a configurable file-type table.
tools.when: Unallocated-space fishing: run it on an image or free-space carve to recover deleted files the live filesystem no longer lists.

tools.name: bulk_extractor
tools.desc: Scans any input byte-by-byte and extracts emails, URLs, credit-card numbers, JPEGs, and JSON to feature files — recursively decoding compressed or encoded blocks without parsing the filesystem.
tools.when: Rapid 'what is in this blob' extraction over images or wiped drives before deep filesystem analysis.

tools.name: scalpel
tools.desc: Filesystem-independent carver using a header/footer definition database — a fast rewrite of foremost's carving engine with tunable per-type carve-size limits.
tools.when: When you need per-type carve-size tuning or an alterative engine for a stubborn image carve beyond foremost defaults.

tools.name: PhotoRec/testdisk
tools.desc: Signature-based recovery of 440+ file formats plus TestDisk for partition-table repair and undelete; no filename reconstruction, but deep salvage on corrupted or reformatted media.
tools.when: Last-ditch recovery from a reformatted or damaged partition or thumb drive in your own hardware lab.

tools.name: plaso/log2timeline
tools.desc: log2timeline extracts timestamped events (filesystem, registry, EVTX, browser, application logs) from an image or mount point into a Plaso storage file; psort turns it into a filtered super-timeline.
tools.when: Build the master super-timeline of an image: collect once with log2timeline, then slice and filter per question with psort.

tools.name: Timesketch
tools.desc: Google's web front-end for collaborative timeline analysis: import Plaso output and search, filter, star, and annotate events in your browser.
tools.when: Turn a giant Plaso timeline into something huntable — collaborative review and annotation for your own case and lab reports.

tools.name: KAPE
tools.desc: Kroll Artifact Parser and Extractor: selects forensically useful artifacts (registry hives, EVTX, Prefetch, MFT, browser files) from a live device or mounted image, then parses them with bundled tools in minutes.
tools.when: Speed triage in your own incident response or lab: point it at a live Windows box or image and get parsed artifacts quickly; extend via community KapeFiles targets.

tools.name: Eric Zimmerman's Tools
tools.desc: Suite of focused parsers — RECmd/Registry Explorer, PECmd (Prefetch), LECmd (LNK), JLECmd (JumpLists), ShellBags, Amcache, MFTECmd — answering execution-timeline questions from individual artifacts.
tools.when: Deep-dive a targeted artifact set: ask 'what executed, when, by whom' via Prefetch, LNK/JumpList, Amcache, and registry traces.

tools.name: Velociraptor
tools.desc: Open-source endpoint visibility and collection platform: deploy lightweight agents, run prebuilt forensic artifacts and fleet-wide hunts via VQL, and pull process, disk, and registry data to a central server.
tools.when: Your own lab or home-network incident: stand up a server, install agents, and answer 'what happened on these hosts' with artifacts and hunts.
tools.install: download velociraptor binary from GitHub releases; run server and deploy agent

tools.name: UAC
tools.desc: Unix-like Artifacts Collector: no-install shell script collecting processes, users, logs, cron, running-file hashes, and bodyfiles from Linux/macOS/BSD/ESXi in order of volatility, packaged for handoff.
tools.when: Rapid live triage on a Linux box you're responding to — run from a USB or read-only medium and hand the archive to your analysis machine.

domains.name: System Hardening, Compliance & Secure Configuration
domains.tagline: Audit, harden, and prove it: system security scans, compliance benchmarks, config automation, and network-service lockdown for defenders securing their own systems.

tools.name: Lynis
tools.desc: Agentless security-auditing tool for Linux, BSD, and macOS that runs 200+ checks across the whole OS, scores everything, and ends with a hardening index, disclosure status, and actionable remediation hints.
tools.when: First pass on any UNIX-like host you own — run a baseline audit, apply the hardening suggestions, then run again to watch the hardening index climb.

tools.name: OpenSCAP
tools.desc: NIST-certified SCAP 1.2 toolkit: loads security content (XCCDF/OVAL data streams) and evaluates or remediates a system against specific profiles from the command line.
tools.when: Repeatable, scriptable compliance evaluations against scap-security-guide content — the profile kills long manual audit checklists.

tools.name: CIS-CAT Pro Assessor
tools.desc: Commercial CIS scanner (SecureSuite membership) that turns CIS Benchmarks into automated scans and compliance score/report output; a free CIS-CAT Lite covers a small set of select benchmarks.
tools.when: Audits that must document conformance to a specific CIS Benchmark version with vendor-supported mapping and reporting.

tools.name: auditd
tools.desc: Linux Audit framework userspace (auditd, auditctl, ausearch) recording privileged actions, file access, and security-relevant events to an immutable log across reboots.
tools.when: Build the audit trail that CIS/STIG rules require before the auditor arrives; verify live rules with auditctl -l and query with ausearch.

tools.name: scap-security-guide
tools.desc: OpenSCAP's official security content: prebuilt SCAP data streams with profiles for CIS, DISA STIG, PCI-DSS, and HIPAA, plus bundled bash and Ansible remediation scripts that actually apply the fixes.
tools.when: Every compliance scan starts here — grab the data stream for your distro, feed it to openscap, review failures, then remediate with the generated scripts.

tools.name: CIS Benchmarks
tools.desc: Free, consensus-built configuration guides (PDF) for hundreds of OS, server, cloud, and application targets — the de-facto hardening standard that auditors and scanners measure against.
tools.when: Hand-hardening a system to a known-good baseline with no scanner available; open the benchmark PDF for your platform and apply the entries manually.
tools.install: preinstalled (web) — free PDF download after registering a CIS account

tools.name: STIG Viewer
tools.desc: Browser database of the entire DISA Security Technical Implementation Guide set — rule-by-rule requirements with severity, CCI/NIST 800-53 mappings, and concrete fix text.
tools.when: Federal or DISA-style compliance: look up the exact configuration a STIG rule demands and its severity before touching config files.

tools.name: ansible-hardening
tools.desc: dev-sec's battle-tested Ansible collection (devsec.hardening) that hardens OS, SSH, nginx, and MySQL/MariaDB at scale, aligned with the InSpec baselines the same team maintains.
tools.when: Apply the same hardening repeatedly to many hosts you manage — idempotent automation beats hand-editing configs on every box.

tools.name: systemd-analyze security
tools.desc: Built-in systemd command that scores each service unit 0-10 on exposure (PrivateTmp, NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem, and more) and lists the exact directives dragging the score down.
tools.when: Zero-install per-service hardening review on any systemd host — run it on your long-running units and tighten the worst offenders.

tools.name: ssh-audit
tools.desc: Audits SSH server and client configuration end-to-end: grades every KEX, cipher, MAC, and host-key algorithm, flags weak or vulnerable combos, and ships per-distro hardening guides.
tools.when: Audit sshd before changing anything, apply the printed hardening guide, then re-scan until the tool reports all-secure.

tools.name: firewalld
tools.desc: Dynamic firewall daemon with zone-based policy, a D-Bus service API, and runtime-vs-permanent config separation; the default firewall manager on RHEL/CentOS/Fedora/SUSE.
tools.when: Host firewalling on RHEL-family systems: open only the services a zone needs and test changes in runtime before committing them permanently.

tools.name: ufw
tools.desc: Ubuntu's uncomplicated frontend over iptables: allow/deny rules for ports and services in a few commands, with sane IPv6 defaults and a status view.
tools.when: Simple proven host firewall on Debian/Ubuntu where firewalld is not the default; same job, less ceremony.

tools.name: Mozilla OpenSSH Config
tools.desc: Reference hardening guide for sshd_config and moduli with Modern/Intermediate/MFA profiles and concrete HostKey, KEX, cipher, and MAC lists for each OpenSSH generation.
tools.when: Write a known-good SSH baseline — put the right profile block into /etc/ssh/sshd_config, then confirm the result with ssh-audit.

domains.name: Honeypots & Deception Technology
domains.tagline: Deception for defenders: fake services, canaries, honeynets, and tripwires placed inside your own estate to catch attackers early and analyze their methods.

tools.name: T-Pot
tools.desc: Bundles 20+ honeypots (Cowrie, Dionaea, Conpot, Snare, Mailoney, LLM-based traps) behind one Docker Compose deploy, with the Elastic stack, Kibana dashboards, Suricata, and a live attack map from the German PSNC/Telekom Security team.
tools.when: When you want a whole instrumented honeynet with dashboards in a weekend instead of wiring sensors together by hand — the standard starting point for a personal or lab deception farm.

tools.name: Modern Honey Network
tools.desc: Centralized server and web UI that deploys honeypot sensors (Cowrie, Dionaea, Conpot, Glastopf) over SSH and aggregates their events via HPFeeds into Elasticsearch for viewing and searching.
tools.when: When you need fleet management of many sensors from one control plane on an older minimal distro — expect friction; the project is effectively unmaintained (Python-2 era) and the torch passes to community forks.

tools.name: Honeyd
tools.desc: Classic low-interaction daemon (Niels Provos) that fabricates thousands of virtual hosts, each with a spoofed nmap/xprobe OS personality and configurable fake TCP/UDP services, on unused IP space.
tools.when: When you want to instrument a whole dark/empty subnet rather than a single box — treat it as legacy research tooling (last original release 2007), built from source in the hobbyist-maintained fork.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/cowrie/honeyd && cd honeyd && mkdir build && cd build && cmake .. && sudo make install

tools.name: HPFeeds
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's authenticated publish-subscribe protocol that ships JSON and binary honeypot events (dionaea.capture, cowrie.sessions, conpot.events,...) from sensors to collectors, MISP, ELK, and SIEMs.
tools.when: The glue beneath MHN, T-Pot, and community honeynets once you run several sensors: subscribe to each honeypot channel so your own analysis stack consumes structured events instead of you scraping logs.

tools.name: Cowrie
tools.desc: Medium-to-high interaction SSH and Telnet honeypot that emulates a fake UNIX filesystem, logs every keystroke and transferred file, records replayable sessions, and can proxy to a real box or use LLMs for dynamic replies.
tools.when: The default SSH honeypot — let credential stuffers 'win' and replay exactly what a post-breach attacker does, from recon commands to download-and-exec malware staging.

tools.name: ssh-honeypot
tools.desc: C-based fake sshd (droberson) that accepts connections and logs IP, username, and password plus HASSH-fingerprints the SSH client — without ever granting a shell.
tools.when: When you care only about brute-force credential and client-fingerprint telemetry with a tiny footprint (popular in attack/defend CTFs), not full shell-level interaction.
tools.install: apt install libssh-dev libjson-c-dev libpcap-dev libssl-dev && make && bin/ssh-honeypot -r ssh-honeypot.rsa

tools.name: sshesame
tools.desc: Go-based fake SSH server that lets any login through, never executes anything on the host, and logs channels, requests, commands, and port-forward activity as JSON.
tools.when: A one-binary lab honeypot or public-facing decoy when you want configurable, JSON-logged session telemetry without emulating a whole filesystem.

tools.name: Beelzebub
tools.desc: Low-code Go deception runtime (a T-Pot 24.04 component) that serves YAML-defined decoy SSH, HTTP, TCP, Telnet, and MCP services, with LLM backends generating convincing real-time replies to keep attackers engaged.
tools.when: When static command emulation is too thin and you want adaptive, high-interaction-deep engagement plus prompt-injection traps for LLM agents — with an OpenAI or local Ollama key in hand.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/mariocandela/beelzebub && cd beelzebub && docker compose up -d

tools.name: kippo
tools.desc: The original medium-interaction SSH honeypot (Upi Tamminen) whose fake 'ubuntu' root shell lured attackers into recording complete shell interactions with replayable TTY logs; Cowrie is its direct fork and successor.
tools.when: Never for fresh deployments — read its Python-2 source and session-replay utilities to understand how Cowrie's fake-shell design evolved, or mine its playback for training labs.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/desaster/kippo && cd kippo && pip install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Dionaea
tools.desc: Nepenthes-successor low-interaction honeypot emulating SMB, FTP, HTTP, MSSQL, MySQL, SIP, UPnP, and more; embeds Python, uses libemu to detect captured shellcode, and stashes malware binaries and connection metadata for analysis.
tools.when: When you want to attract self-spreading worms and malware that rips over SMB/FTP/MS-RPC and capture their payloads, complementing a credential-focused SSH honeypot.

tools.name: Snare (w/ Tanner)
tools.desc: Glastopf's successor: SNARE clones real web pages into sensor traps and forwards every request to TANNER, a central classification service that evaluates the attack and decides the reply — dynamic camouflage across many sensors.
tools.when: When you want realistic web deception with a central 'brain': point several SNARE clones at one TANNER to store, classify, and steer web-application attack responses in one place.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/mushorg/snare && cd snare && pip3 install -r requirements.txt && python3 setup.py install

tools.name: Glastopf
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's original web-application honeypot that emulated vulnerability types (LFI/RFI/SQLi) with a built-in PHP sandbox and Google dork luring; archived, with maintainers pointing to SNARE/TANNER as the successor.
tools.when: Historical study only: inspect the PHP-sandbox emulation and dork-collection design to learn how modern web honeypots behave; do not deploy to fresh systems today.

tools.name: Canarytokens
tools.desc: Thinkst's free hosted (or self-hosted Docker) tripwire factory generating DNS, URL, document (PDF/Word), AWS-key, QR-code, and Slack tokens that alert by email/webhook the instant someone touches them.
tools.when: When a full honeypot is overkill: sprinkle a few fake DNS names, URLs, or documents across AD, share drives, and public infra for cheap, near-instant detection of unauthorized access.
tools.install: preinstalled (canarytokens.org) — self-host: git clone https://github.com/thinkst/canarytokens-docker && cd canarytokens-docker && docker compose up

tools.name: OpenCanary
tools.desc: Thinkst's open-source multi-protocol honeypot daemon (SSH, telnet, HTTP, FTP, SNMP, SMB, RDP, MySQL, and more) that fires syslog, email, Slack, and webhook alerts on any probe; the OSS sibling of the commercial Thinkst Canary.
tools.when: Drop a near-zero-footprint daemon onto a jump host, file server, or DMZ and get alerting on unexpected interaction across ~10 common protocols at once, without standing up a sensor farm.

tools.name: Conpot
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's ICS/SCADA honeypot emulating Modbus, S7, BACnet, EtherNet/IP, IEC-104, SNMP, and HTTP HMI stacks to look like a real industrial process, with tunable service response delays for realism.
tools.when: When you want to detect and profile targeting of OT/SCADA or smart-infrastructure equipment — replant a fake PLC/HMI on your own network before adversaries reach real controllers.

tools.name: RIoTPot
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's IoT and OT honeypot: a hybrid proxy that fronts emulated services — SSH, Telnet, HTTP, Modbus, MQTT, CoAP — and can route interactions to any backend honeypot, managed through a small web UI.
tools.when: When your focus is IoT/OT protocol coverage (MQTT, CoAP, Modbus) and you want a Honeynet-endorsed, plugin-architected emulator instead of gluing single-service traps — expect a young, source-built project.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/honeynet/riotpot && cd riotpot && make

domains.name: Malware Analysis & Reverse Engineering
domains.tagline: Static and dynamic analysis of samples you recovered — honeypot catches, quarantined files, lab targets, and public samples — to extract IOCs and understand behavior. Analyze, don't distribute.

tools.name: CAPEv2
tools.desc: The actively maintained Cuckoo successor (Cape Sandbox): detonates a sample in an isolated Windows VM, instruments behavior, auto-unpacks, and extracts ransomware/botnet configuration via YARA-driven debugger hooks.
tools.when: Default detonation engine for any sample you regained — drop it in the lab, read the process/network/file report, and get an unpacked payload plus extracted config out.
tools.install: sudo bash cape2.sh all (from the CAPEv2 installer on Ubuntu 24.04 + Windows 10/11 guest)

tools.name: Hybrid Analysis
tools.desc: CrowdStrike Falcon Sandbox's free-to-use cloud detonation service that returns a full behavioral report with process activity, dropped files, and network indicators for a submitted file.
tools.when: A no-infrastructure second opinion on a publicly shared sample or one you are cleared to share — remember public submission exposes the file, so never upload anything sensitive.
tools.install: preinstalled (web, free account + API vetting for keys)

tools.name: Cuckoo Sandbox
tools.desc: The original open-source automated malware-analysis sandbox (pip-installable) and architectural ancestor of CAPE — repository archived April 2021 and unmaintained since, with a stalled community rewrite.
tools.when: Learning the plugin/API/signature model that CAPE builds on, or reading old published research — treat it as a museum reference, not a new deployment.

tools.name: YARA
tools.desc: Pattern-matching language for describing and classifying malware families (byte strings, regexes, hex wildcards, PE/module conditionals); the signature format AV engines and sandboxes consume. The C engine is in maintenance mode — the Rust rewrite YARA-X is the actively-evolving successor.
tools.when: Fingerprint a sample and hunt the same family across your recovered-file collection; the community rule base (yara-forge, Malpedia) gives instant triage hits.

tools.name: capa
tools.desc: Mandiant FLARE tool that statically identifies what a PE, ELF, .NET, or shellcode blob can do — C2, keylogging, anti-VM tricks, MITRE ATT&CK techniques — from its code, not just strings.
tools.when: Ask 'what does this binary do?' in one command — run it on the unpacked payload, or on a CAPE report to match capabilities to captured behavior.

tools.name: Detect-It-Easy (DIE)
tools.desc: Cross-platform signature + heuristic detector (GUI 'die', console 'diec') that identifies compilers, packers, protectors, and file format anomalies across PE, ELF, Mach-O, and more.
tools.when: Seconds-long first pass on any sample: packer/protector verdict tells you whether unpacking is needed before you pull in a reversing suite.
tools.install: Download the die/diec release from GitHub (or 'choco install die' on Windows)

tools.name: oledump
tools.desc: Didier Stevens' OLE/Compound-File analyzer that lists streams inside Office documents, flags streams containing VBA macros (M indicator), decompresses macro source, and dumps embedded objects — without running the file.
tools.when: Triage malicious Office attachments (maldocs) recovered from email gateways or inboxes: find the macro, deobfuscate it, and dump the embedded payload it builds.

tools.name: ExifTool
tools.desc: Reads and writes metadata for hundreds of file types — Office document properties (author, edit timestamps), PDF, and EXIF/XMP in lure images. Not an executable analyzer: for PE headers use DIE or file with pefile.
tools.when: Pull provenance metadata out of document and image lures (who authored the misdelivered/social-engineering file) before the payload analysis starts.

tools.name: x64dbg
tools.desc: Open-source user-mode Windows debugger (x32dbg + x64dbg in one package) with an IDA-like interface, API breakpoints, memory/register views, and a scriptable plugin engine — the standard debugger for Windows malware.
tools.when: Step through an unpacked Windows sample inside FLARE VM: break on suspicious API calls, dump decrypted buffers, and unwind anti-analysis logic.
tools.install: Download the latest snapshot from GitHub releases and run x96dbg.exe

tools.name: Process Monitor
tools.desc: Microsoft Sysinternals freeware that records real-time file system, registry, process/thread, and DLL activity for the whole system, with non-destructive filtering, process trees, and boot-time logging.
tools.when: Watch exactly what a detonating sample touches — files written, keys created, processes spawned — in your own analysis VM, and save the trace as evidence.

tools.name: GDB
tools.desc: The GNU debugger: sets breakpoints, inspects registers/memory, and single-steps program execution — the x64dbg equivalent when the sample is a Linux ELF (honeypot binaries, shared libraries).
tools.when: Debug a regained Linux malware sample or dropper natively when a Windows-only debugger cannot touch it; pair with pwndbg/GEF for readable state.

tools.name: Ghidra
tools.desc: NSA's free reverse-engineering suite: interactive disassembler plus a quality decompiler emitting C-like pseudocode, with a Python scriptable API for automating config extraction and large batches.
tools.when: Primary static analysis tool for an unpacked payload you want to fully understand — the decompiler output reads close to source and capa runs on its analysis.
tools.install: Download the current release zip from the GitHub releases page, unzip, and run ./ghidraRun

tools.name: radare2
tools.desc: Command-line reverse-engineering framework with analyzers, disassemblers, ESIL emulation, and r2pipe scripting for one-terminal headless analysis of ELF/PE/Mach-O and shellcode.
tools.when: Scripted or headless reversing on the analysis box — batch-analyze a sample set, grep for crypto constants, or automate unpacking without opening a GUI.

tools.name: rizin
tools.desc: Community fork of radare2 aimed at a cleaner, better-tested engine while staying command-compatible, with rz-pipe and Rust bindings; powers the Cutter GUI.
tools.when: The same CLI workflow as radare2 when you prefer the faster-moving fork or plan to script via its language bindings.

tools.name: Cutter
tools.desc: Qt GUI front-end over the rizin engine giving point-and-click disassembly, patching, graph views, and annotation in a visual workspace; ships native plugins including a Ghidra decompiler integration.
tools.when: Visual exploration and annotating of a sample's functions and strings when you prefer a mouse-driven workflow over r2's terminal.

tools.name: IDA Free
tools.desc: Hex-Rays' free tier of the industry-standard disassembler: x86/x64 support, cloud-based decompiler, and the IDA workflow at no cost — but limited architectures and an account-based download since v9.
tools.when: You want IDA's exact toolchain and shortcuts for a Windows x86/x64 sample without a license; on other arches or for local decompilation, Ghidra is freer.
tools.install: Register at hex-rays.com/ida-free and download the freeware

tools.name: REMnux
tools.desc: The Linux toolkit for malware analysis (Lenny Zeltser): a curated Ubuntu-based distro (also available as Docker images) with YARA, DIE, oledump, capa, radare2, and dozens of analysis helpers preinstalled.
tools.when: Your malware-analysis workbench — run it as a VM or pull individual containerized tools so you analyze from a vetted, isolated toolkit instead of your main OS.
tools.install: Import the REMnux VM OVA from remnux.org, or 'docker pull remnux/remnux-distro'

tools.name: FLARE VM
tools.desc: Mandiant's scripted Windows analysis environment (Chocolatey + Boxstarter) that provisions a Win10/11 VM with x64dbg, Ghidra, IDA, ProcMon, process tools, and unpackers tuned for Windows malware.
